Industry observers note that this set earns a spot for the sheer amount of resistance it offers—up to 300 pounds, more than any other kit on our list. That’s more than enough tension to challenge even advanced lifters. HPYGN also sells lighter-weight bundles at lower prices, but every option comes with the basics: a travel pouch, door anchor, handles, and ankle/wrist straps.

In a recent development, with over 10,000 reviews and a 4.5-star average, it’s an Amazon favorite. Some users note that bands have snapped under strain or that the listed resistance feels exaggerated, though the latter is subjective. On the flip side, many reviewers praise the sturdier build. One wrote: “I was pleasantly surprised that the gear looked like the ads and worked well. I bought it because of the metal carabiners that make it easy to change bands, and I wasn’t disappointed.”.

You’ll need a solid anchor point to get the most out of these, and long-term durability is a question mark. Still, if you’re trying to ditch your gym membership or want a heavy-duty band system for travel, HPYGN’s kit is a worthy pick. It’s affordable, versatile, and capable of potentially replacing machines and free weights.

In a recent development, this rig gives you a little more than just the bands. We put this setup to the test, and found it to be super fun and intuitive to use. You can think of the Gorilla Bow as a hybrid tool that combines the benefits of resistance bands with a bow-style bar, which allows for a lot more versatility than a resistance band alone.

Industry observers note that the unique bow design accommodates up to 300 pounds of resistance (just to start, you can get heavier models) that you can use to target just about every muscle group. The bow itself is made out of aircraft aluminum while the resistance bands are double-wall latex, resulting in a durable, lightweight, and portable build.

Sources indicate that resistance is adjustable, with the bow supporting up to four bands at a time so you can customize your resistance to meet your needs. The set comes with one original 56-inch bow, four Gorilla Bands (10, 20, 30 and 50-pounds), a band wrap, and a 30-day all-access membership to Gorilla Bow's virtual training platform. It's pricey, yes. But it packs a lot more usability than your average standalone resistance band.

Mini bands are a staple for warm-ups and recovery work, often wrapped around the knees for lateral walks or used to cue better glute and abductor activation during squats. Titan’s version is a little different. Designed initially as attachments for the brand’s Vice Grip Trainer, these bands double as standalone mini bands. And because they’re built for machine resistance, they’re thicker, more durable, and provide far greater tension than typical minis.

The resistance ranges from 15 pounds up to 120 pounds, which means the lightest bands are great for activation drills, while the heavy green band can push your lateral walks well past warm-up territory.

The catch is price. At nearly $50, these cost significantly more than most mini-band sets, and their uses are inherently limited compared to looped or tube bands. Still, the build quality is excellent, and the extra resistance opens the door for more challenging work than you’ll get with cheaper, flimsier bands. If you’re willing to invest once for a set that won’t wear out promptly, Titan’s mini bands are a “buy once, cry once” purchase.

Rogue is synonymous with quality in the fitness equipment space, and its tube resistance bands live up to the reputation. If you’re looking for bands to actually build workouts around—not just warm up with—these are among the best. The textured rubber handles stand out: they’re coated in a knurl-like pattern that gives you a secure grip, even when your hands get sweaty.

I noted that REP Fitness’s loop bands were long at 38 inches, and Rogue’s bands clock even longer at an elastic length of 48 inches. However, the length does allow you to perform overhead presses, lateral raises, and kickbacks with the bands. To increase the tension, loop the band around a squat rack or pole and take a few steps back. (Though Rogue warns users not to overstretch the band.) Each band is a standalone product, so you can’t clip multiple elastic tubes to a pair of handles, as with other models.

Price-wise, individual bands cost a bit more than some competitors, but Rogue makes up for it with bundle pricing. A light set (bands 0-2) runs $36.50, the heavy set (3-5) is $45, and the full collection is $75. Considering the quality and the savings versus buying separately, the sets are where the real value lies. For those who want tube bands tough enough for serious training, Rogue delivers.

In a recent development, these resistance bands feature four tubes braided together to create a durable workout tool that can stand up to your toughest sessions. We love that customers can choose from five resistance levels, ranging from feather-light to heavy-duty, and select the perfect size and tension based on their preferences and fitness level. We found the handles comfortable, featuring a protective sleeve and grommet reinforcement which helps to ensure a solid grip.

While they excel in mobility work, don't expect crazy heavy resistance. They come in five resistance levels, from 'very light' to 'very heavy', ranging from 3 to 27 pounds. The various levels also differ in length, ranging from the 44-inch very light cord to the very heavy 53-inch cord, so you can pick the size and tension right for you.

If you want to go all in with resistance bands, WHATAFIT offers five bands (10, 20, 30, 40, 50-pound listed resistances), handles, ankle straps, a door anchor, and a carrying pouch. Some bundles even come with additional looped or mini bands. You’re not going to get much closer to having a complete gym in your home—especially for under $40—than with this set.

Industry observers note that the set is also wildly popular: With a 4.6-star average and over 34,000 reviews—more than any other band on this list—it has the people’s approval. You can stack the bands for more precise resistance, which makes progressive overload easier and mimics the flexibility you’d get in a commercial gym. As one reviewer put it: “The materials feel high-quality and durable, and the bands have held up really well so far. I’ve used them for upper body, lower body, and core training without any concerns. Plus, the whole set is compact and easy to store or travel with.”.

According to recent reports, what holds it back slightly is that these bands are serviceable, not premium. While natural latex is great for elasticity, it can degrade over time with sweat, sun, and repeated stretch cycles, so expect some wear. That stated, for the price, this set offers a wide breadth of use and works well for someone building up strength or who needs a versatile “one-stop” band kit.

It has been revealed that your most notable consideration should be how you plan to use your resistance bands—for solo workouts, to add resistance to exercises, to help you with dips or pull-ups, or to warm up before your lifts. No one band will perfectly check every box.

Recent findings suggest that most resistance bands are made from latex and rubber (or some combination of the two) and use plastic parts for accessories like handles and door anchors. (If you have a latex allergy, there are latex-free resistance bands.) So we’re not going to list materials as a significant consideration.

Likewise, the bands in this guide are all similar in price, with no major outliers. Premium and/or unique band designs cost more, but expect to pay between $20 and $70 for bands. The price scales based on the band resistance and whether or not you’re buying a set. Below are the top three things you should consider when shopping around for a new resistance band.

It has been revealed that the type of band you buy dictates the kind of workouts you can perform. Here’s a quick breakdown of the band styles you’ll see, save for a few unique models, most of which are on this list.

Industry observers note that also referred to as super bands, these are the quintessential resistance bands that most manufacturers sell. Because the band is a single loop, you have to get creative in performing specific exercises, but you can target most major muscles with a looped band. You can also wrap them around pull-up bars, barbells, and machines to change the resistance profile of an exercise.

According to recent reports, popular in physical therapy offices, mini bands are an excellent tool for activating the smaller muscles in your hips, legs, upper back, and shoulders. They can’t support your bodyweight and they don’t stretch far enough to allow for squats, presses, or curls. Think of these as a warm-up tool, not a workout replacement.

Industry observers note that these bands are defined by a single tube of rubber with a handle on each end (usually). These bands give you the most freedom of movement, and the handles allow you to press and row more efficiently (compared to looped bands).

It has been revealed that some bands cite a single poundage versus a range. If a band lists its resistance as between 20 and 60 force, you’ll experience 20 pounds of resistance when the band is least stretched and 60 pounds at the most stretched position. Squatting with a 50-pound band doesn’t feel the same as squatting with a 50-pound dumbbell, either, since the force you’re resisting is literally changing with every inch you move.

Industry observers note that to track your progress effectively, find a band that has you reaching within one to three reps of failure for your desired rep range. Stick with that band until the reps feel easier, and then move up to the next heaviest band you have. Progressing with bands isn’t as easy as with free weights and machines, but you'll make gains as long as you’re basing your effort on training intensity and not weight.

Sources indicate that resistance bands can be dangerous. If they snap while doing assisted pull-ups or a face pull, you’ll fall or injure your eyes or face. No band is wear-proof, so it’s essential to use them responsibly: don’t overstretch, inspect them regularly for tears, and avoid anchoring them against textured surfaces like the knurling on a barbell, which creates friction that weakens the material.

Manufacturers use different strategies to improve longevity. Some bands are built from layered latex for added reinforcement, while others encase the elastic in a protective sleeve that reduces wear and shields the user from a whip-like snap mid-rep. These features can’t eliminate risk, but they can extend the lifespan of your bands and make training safer.

As a longtime fitness journalist and NASM-certified trainer, I have spent years using resistance bands in a variety of exercise scenarios. For this story, I worked in tandem with the team at Men's Health, including Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, CSCS, and Fitness and Commerce Editor Charles Thorp, NASM. We also recruited the help of MH Strength in Diversity members Juan Guadarrama, CSCS and Eric Sung, CSCS to gather diverse perspectives on the topic.

Industry observers note that we used our collective experience to put together a testing pool by putting the most popular designs that we could put up against newly introduced offerings from classic brands as well as newcomers to the market. Both historically and in the pursuit of this story, we used these designs during band-only workouts, athletic movements, and to advance fundamental movements like the deadlift. The selections above represent the best resistance bands that you can buy now.

We asked Strength in Diversity member Eric Sung about his favorite ways to incorporate resistance bands with clients and in his own training.

"The banded rear delt fly is great exercise to do as a warm up to prepare your body before an upper body session," says Sung. "Grab the band, hold it out in front of you, stretch it across your upper chest and try to resist the band as much and slowly as you can.".

According to recent reports, if you're looking to get started in training lower body plyometrics, put band-assisted squat jumps on your radar. "Tie a band to a high anchor, grab each end of it, assume your squat stance, and focus on jumping as high as you can with the assistance of the band. This is a great entry point," he adds.

For more ideas, check out our list of 12 resistance band workouts you can do at home.

Recent findings suggest that similar to free weights, resistance bands help create tension and place stress on the muscles, explains Sung. However, resistance bands assist in efforts to build muscle and strength in a few unique ways.

Recent findings suggest that because they deliver more resistance as you stretch them further, they offer a different challenge than free weights. This means your muscles face the most load and tension at the top of every exercise. For example, the top of a resistance band pushup is a challenge; the top of a bodyweight pushup is a position of rest.

In a recent development, another way resistance bands help build strength is by assisting in movements that an individual cannot yet complete at baseline standards, explains Guadarrama. "It allows athletes to move through the full range of motion and acquire neuromuscular capacity," he explains. "Over time the body can adapt, learn the movement, and build the strength needed for the unassisted effort.".

Bands can also be attached to plates and kettlebells to add more resistance to the eccentric or concentric phases of a given movement, explains Guadarrama. "Each of these methods has benefits to biomechanical advantages and providing variance in stress," he says.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The US Treasury could be required to publicly verify its Bitcoin holdings under legislation advancing through Congress.

The House Financial Services Committee formally reported the amended American Reserve Modernization Act of 2026 on Nov. 24, placing it on the House Union Calendar for the full chamber to consider.

The legislative development follows the committee's Sept. 16 vote, when lawmakers approved the measure 28-21.

Industry observers note that introduced in May by Republican Rep. Nick Begich, the bill would give statutory backing to the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve that President Donald Trump established through a March 2025 executive order.

Under Section 6 of the legislation, Treasury would establish a proof-of-reserves system using public cryptographic attestations and publish annual reports detailing its Bitcoin holdings, transactions, and control of the associated private keys.

Treasury would also appoint an independent auditor specializing in cryptographic attestations to verify the accuracy of its disclosures. The US Comptroller General would regularly review the reserve's management and audits.

The proposed requirements would give investors a clearer picture of how much Bitcoin the federal government has accumulated as a strategic asset.

Trump's executive order required federal agencies to account for their digital asset holdings within 30 days, but directed those disclosures to Treasury and the President's Working Group on Digital Asset Markets rather than the public.

H.R. 8957 would require a broad internal agency inventory and a public report on Bitcoin deposited in the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve.

The annual public report would detail reserve holdings, transactions and control of private keys.

The bill leaves the cryptographic proof method open. Court and forfeiture records would remain relevant to title and third-party claims.

Maps the roles of Sections 3, 4, 6 and 7 of H.R. 8957, along with the third-party claim process in 21 U.S.C. § 853(n).

The bill leaves the cryptographic proof method open. Court and forfeiture records would remain relevant to title and third-party claims.

The distinction is significant because government-linked blockchain wallets can contain seized Bitcoin that remains subject to legal proceedings or restitution claims. Cryptographic verification, combined with independent accounting, could help establish how much Bitcoin actually belongs to the reserve.

Beyond transparency, the legislation would formalize the federal government's long-term Bitcoin accumulation strategy and limit its ability to liquidate reserve assets.

Federal agencies would have 60 days after enactment to submit comprehensive inventories of their cryptocurrency holdings to Treasury.

Sources indicate that the department would then have six months from enactment to establish the statutory Bitcoin reserve and a separate stockpile for other digital assets. Agencies would have another 30 days to transfer eligible holdings.

Federally owned Bitcoin deposited into the reserve would face a minimum 20-year holding period beginning at enactment, during which Treasury could neither sell the assets nor pledge them as collateral.

Two years before that period expires, Treasury would recommend whether to continue holding Bitcoin or begin gradually reducing its position. Potential sales could reach 10% of reserve assets over any two-year period following the lockup.

Meanwhile, the legislation directs the Treasury and Commerce departments to evaluate ways of expanding the reserve without increasing the national debt or imposing additional costs on taxpayers.

The six-month study would examine potential exchanges of other government-held cryptocurrencies for Bitcoin, additional asset forfeitures and partnerships with states, private entities and international counterparts.

However, the legislation faces a tightening congressional timetable. With the 119th Congress approaching its January conclusion, lawmakers have limited time to secure House and Senate approval.

Failure to pass the measure before the current Congress ends would require its reintroduction in the next session, leaving America's Bitcoin reserve governed by executive action without the proposed public auditing requirements.

Bitcoin Miners Go 98 Minutes Without Finding a Single Block

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (489 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: U

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, bitcoin miners experienced their longest dry spell since July on Nov.
  • That's the third time in 2026 that miners have gone this long without finding a block.
  • For anyone trying to get Bitcoin transactions confirmed shortly after the previous block, the gap meant waiting more than an hour and a half.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, bitcoin miners experienced their longest dry spell since July on Nov. 26. According to Galaxy's Alex Thorn, it took Bitcoin miners 98 minutes and 19 seconds to find the next block.

That's the third time in 2026 that miners have gone this long without finding a block. The wait ended at 18:28 UTC on Thursday.

For anyone trying to get Bitcoin transactions confirmed shortly after the previous block, the gap meant waiting more than an hour and a half.

Even if you paid a very high transaction fee, you would still have to wait until a miner found the next block before your transaction could receive its first confirmation.

Thursday's gap was the 69th longest since 2011, according to Galaxy Research. It was just three minutes shy of the threshold for the top 50.

In a recent development, and this year's other long gap lasted nearly two hours. On July 6, miners took 112 minutes and 26 seconds to find the next block (number 956,953). That was the 19th longest gap on record, according to Galaxy.

Bitcoin automatically adjusts mining difficulty every 2,016 blocks to keep the average block interval at around 10 minutes.

It has been revealed that however,  blocks sometimes are found seconds apart. Other times, it takes well over an hour for the next block to be found.

At any given mining difficulty, the chance that a single attempt to find a block will succeed is incredibly small.

If miners have spent 90 minutes trying to find the next block, the chance of succeeding on the next attempt is the same as it was on the first attempt.

So the expected time until the next block is found is still 10 minutes, even if it's already been 90 minutes since the last block was found. That's assuming the network's total computing power and mining difficulty remain unchanged.

Assuming an average block interval of 10 minutes, Thorn remarked you could expect a gap of at least 98 minutes and 19 seconds about once every 18,600 block intervals.

That means such a gap should occur roughly once every four months, based on an average of about 144 blocks per day.

Galaxy examined 877,290 block intervals going back to Jan. 1, 2011.

Researchers identified 1,948 intervals where at least an hour had passed between the timestamps of successive blocks.

According to recent reports, however, Galaxy flagged 97 of those intervals because an adjacent block had a timestamp that was off by at least 10 minutes. This raised questions about the actual length of those gaps.

The longest recorded interval is particularly interesting.

On Nov. 30, 2011, block 155,290 seemingly marked the end of a 144-minute-and-50-second gap.

However, the miner who found the next block had set its timestamp back by 65 minutes.

After excluding apparent timestamp errors, the longest gap was 141 minutes and one second, recorded on Oct. 13, 2011.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A Tesla Model 3 drove into an overturned box truck on I-75 near Naples, Florida, killing two of its passengers and a man who had stopped to help.
  • In a recent development, police and local media covered the May 31 crash as a truck wreck in the dark, and none of it mentioned a driver-assist system.
  • on Sunday, May 31, 2026, the 31-year-old driver of a 2014 Freightliner lost the road near the Pine Ridge Road exit in Collier County, steered back onto southbound I-75, and flipped it, according to the Florida Highway Patrol.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A Tesla Model 3 drove into an overturned box truck on I-75 near Naples, Florida, killing two of its passengers and a man who had stopped to help. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators notes Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, at 71 mph.

In a recent development, police and local media covered the May 31 crash as a truck wreck in the dark, and none of it mentioned a driver-assist system. It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data, and it lands as Tesla’s monthly crash count hits another record.

Just before 4 a.m. on Sunday, May 31, 2026, the 31-year-old driver of a 2014 Freightliner lost the road near the Pine Ridge Road exit in Collier County, steered back onto southbound I-75, and flipped it, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The overturned truck ended up blocking the center and outside lanes.

In a recent development, jonathan Garcia Arias, a 25-year-old Naples man and former Marine, was driving by in a BMW. He pulled over and got out to help the truck driver.

Recent findings suggest that then a southbound 2023 Tesla with five young men from Naples inside came up on the scene. FHP’s report says the front of the Tesla hit the underside of the overturned truck and Garcia Arias. Two of the Tesla’s passengers, aged 18 and 19, died at the scene, and Garcia Arias died later in the hospital. The 20-year-old driver and two more passengers were seriously hurt.

Recent findings suggest that A few days later, FHP used the crash as a warning about stopping near wrecks on the interstate. Senior Trooper Kenn Watson stated the Tesla driver would have seen only the truck’s underside, with “no lights, no reflectors, nothing warning them.”.

It has been revealed that so that’s the official story. A dark obstacle, a driver who couldn’t see it in time. Nobody said a word about Autopilot.

It has been revealed that under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone was killed or hurt. Tesla filed one for this crash.

It has been revealed that it identifies the car as a 2023 Model 3 on a highway, flags a traffic incident on the roadway, and marks the automation “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged.” That means Tesla confirmed through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 71 mph and a fatality, lists the Florida Highway Patrol as the investigating agency, and states it learned of the crash from police and the media.

Then it blacks out the crash narrative, the software version, and whether the road was within the system’s approved operating domain, all as “confidential business information.” That’s the same redaction Tesla applies to 99.9% of its reports.

The report also surfaced late. Tesla filed it as a 5-Day report, the urgent category for fatal crashes, but it didn’t land until Tesla’s September filings, more than three months after the crash. And Tesla lists law enforcement as one of the ways it found out about it.

Recent findings suggest that how we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 07:56 UTC, which converts to 3:56 a.m. in Florida, two minutes off the 3:54 a.m. in FHP’s report. The city, the highway, the 2023 model year, the month and the fatal outcome all line up, and it’s the only fatal Tesla driver-assist report in Naples that month. It’s the same crash.

Recent findings suggest that A Tesla on driver-assist going highway speed into the underside of a big truck, in the dark, in Florida. If that sounds familiar, it should.

In 2016, Joshua Brown was killed near Williston when his Model S on Autopilot drove under a tractor-trailer crossing the highway. In 2019, Jeremy Banner died in Delray Beach when his Model 3 on Autopilot went under a trailer at 68 mph and had its roof sheared off. In both crashes, neither the driver nor the system braked.

Recent findings suggest that trooper Watson’s point was that a human couldn’t see the truck. But a big, unlit obstacle sitting across two lanes at night is exactly the kind of thing a driver-assist system is supposed to catch, and Tesla now sells FSD as nearly ready to drive with nobody watching. And an attentive driver could clearly see it, as the BMW driver did, and stop before the Tesla arrived.

It has been revealed that we want to be fair about what the data doesn’t prove. “Engaged within 30 seconds” is the reporting trigger. Tesla’s 71 mph may be a telematics snapshot rather than the impact speed. And with the software version redacted, we can’t say whether this was Autopilot or FSD.

The NHTSA release that surfaced this crash, covering filings through October 15, also set a fresh monthly high. Tesla reported 264 driver-assist crashes in September 2026, beating July’s 236, which was itself a record. That’s up from 135 in March.

September may still grow as late reports come in. This Naples crash shows how late they can be.

Our merged dataset now holds 4,669 Tesla driver-assist crash reports since 2019, 69 of them flagged fatal. The same release added two other fatal reports, both “Verified Engaged” and both covered locally with no mention of driver-assist: a Model Y that hit a tree and burned in El Dorado Hills, California, killing three, and a Model X that hit a signal pole in Naples on September 30, killing a passenger. We’ll lay those out separately.

Industry observers note that three people died on I-75, including a man who got out of his car to help a stranger. Tesla knows its driver-assist was on, knows the speed, holds the telematics, and filed a federal report saying so. Then it sealed everything that would explain what the car did, and the public got a story about a dark truck.

That's what happens when the system has to identify all objects in the camera frame before it can start to estimate the objects position and then relative distance and then relative velocity. Unrecognizable objects will destroy all your logic. This is a design failure and not something Tesla can actually fix.

Compare that to radars and lidars that directly measure distances and relative velocities of everything in front of the car, regardless of what it is. That is a far better approach because you do not want the car the impact objects on its trajectory regardless of what those objects turn out to be.

Tesla’s whole pitch for FSD is that the car sees better than you do, and yet, Tesla vehicles on Autopilot and FSD keep crashing on stationary objects on the highway. It’s the same failure that killed Joshua Brown and Jeremy Banner years ago. If the system saw the truck and the driver overrode it, Tesla should say so. It was quick to do that in the Katy crash when the data helped it. If the system didn’t see it, that’s a safety defect regulators and owners need to know about.

Either way, the redaction protects Tesla, not the people on the road. It’s the same pattern we found in Vineland and in July’s four fatal crashes, and the crash count keeps setting records.

Sources indicate that we’re asking the Florida Highway Patrol for the full crash report, whether its investigators got Tesla’s raw vehicle data, and whether they even knew the system was engaged. If they didn’t, the only party that knows what this car did is the one that sealed the file.

Back in the day, a sweatsuit was all about comfort. It wasn’t so much a fashion staple, but the kind of thing to throw on and lounge in. With Y2K style back in vogue, matching sweatsuits are more commonplace than ever—just with a little less sparkle than the ones previously sported by icons like Paris Hilton and J.Lo in the early 2000s. And, with the rise of athleisure, these simple sweats have gotten the luxury treatment: they’re softer, more flattering, and pricier than ever.

Whether you’re the kind of person who considers it a cozy wardrobe essential, or you’re just looking to treat yourself to something comfortable to wear around the house, there have never been more choices when it comes to the best matching sweatsuits. Since we’re heading into winter (and Black Friday is just around the corner!), Women’s Health editors tested the most popular styles.

Here are our thoughts on the matching sets after months of lounging in them, working from home in them, and even wearing them to work.

Oner Active Foundations Zip Up Hoodie.

Oner Active Foundations Sweatpants.

Recent findings suggest that oner Active’s workout clothes have had our hearts at WH for a while. That’s why we were excited to put their loungewear to the test. Associate Health and Fitness editor Addison Aloian wore this set while traveling, chilling at home, and even working behind the scenes on a photoshoot.

It has been revealed that “I absolutely love this set from Oner,” she indicates. She loves it for its comfort, warmth, and versatility (Aloian says she knows she could wear it outside in the chilly NYC winter, layer it under her ski clothes, or pop it on over leggings for her warm-up at the gym). “But the standout feature is the color,” Aloian says. “So many sweat sets are gray or black, but the turquoise is stunning and makes it a standout in my closet when I want a monochromatic moment.” She opted for the “oil blue” color, but Oner also has options like alpine green and toasted red, plus your neutral staples.

It’s also one of the more affordable options we tested—and on sale for half off this Black Friday. But that doesn’t mean it skimps on quality: The material feels super plush since it’s made from 67% cotton and 33% polyester, for a super plush feel that doesn’t pill or shed after one wash.

Sources indicate that the set’s one flaw? The bottoms are a little long. At 5 '1, Aloian claims she’d love a “short” option as well. Oner does offer a “long” length, though, for the taller girlies.

Old Navy Bounce Fleece Half-Zip Pullover Sweatshirt.

Old Navy High-Waisted Bounce Fleece Jogger Sweatpants.

In a world of expensive sweat sets, Old Navy’s Bounce Fleece line provides a budget-friendly—and stylish—option. “You’d never know these are super affordable,” claims Fitness editor Cori Ritchey. They hold their own with the rest of the pricier sets from their fit to their feel.

The highlight for Ritchey is the material, a mix of polyester, rayon, and spandex. “It moves with you, and the fabric feels like it breathes compared to other sweatsuits that feel too heavy and hot.” One small caveat: Be sure to follow the wash instructions and keep your cycle on cold and gentle, tumble dry low, and keep the garments inside out. Ritchey indicates she noticed a bit of pilling after the first wash, but says that after following the wash instructions during the next few washes, the set stayed in great shape.

In a recent development, the half-zip and jogger combo makes for a put-together look and is cozy enough for traveling, running errands, or lounging around the house, Ritchey indicates. The set comes in plenty of neutral colors, plus some fun ones like orchid. It’s also the first on our list that doesn’t have a prominent logo, for anyone who wants a clean-looking set with no branding. Another point for Old Navy: It’s the most size-inclusive on the list. Sizing goes from XS to 4XL, with regular, tall, and petite options.

Alo Accolade Crew Neck Pullover.

Alo is another longtime favorite at WH. The brand is known for its cozy, stylish (and premium-priced) loungewear. The fit is what we love most. The set, which comes in over a dozen colors, has an oversized feel, yet still manages to look intentional, claims Deputy Features editor Carina Hsieh. “Unlike other sweatsuits, this one doesn’t look or feel unflattering or sloppy,” she says. She especially likes how it falls on her shoulders.

In a recent development, it’s also the “perfect transition-weather sweatsuit.” The French terry material is made up of 65% cotton and 35% polyester, for a “really soft, thick, and high-quality” feel. The fabric doesn’t feel ultra-heavy, though, so it’s a great pick for fall and spring when you might overheat in thicker sets. Another perk? The pants have pockets.

However, the sizing isn’t the most intuitive. Hsieh, who is typically a small or medium in other brands, is an extra-extra small in these pants. The pants also run a bit long. Hsieh states sizing down is likely the way to go for this set.

Aritzia Cozy Sweatfleece Mega Funnel Neck.

Aritzia Cozy Sweatfleece Mega Jogger.

According to recent reports, I had been hearing great things about Aritzia’s Sweatfleece line, and after testing for over a month, I can attest that it’s truly the coziest sweat set I’ve worn. Made from 78% cotton and 22% polyester, the material is soft with a fleece-lined interior. They’ll definitely keep you warm; that fleece inside is perfect for chilly temps. But they don’t feel too heavy. The material is still breathable, and I don’t get overheated when I’m wearing them.

Sources indicate that I also love the look of this set, especially with the funnel/mockneck style—which is very on-trend. I have been wearing the suit when I work from home, and it makes me feel put together and chic, even though I’m in the coziest clothes I own. I’m also a runner, and I've noticed that this is the first thing I want to put on after I shower post-run. It’s the ultimate comfy outfit for recovery.

Sources indicate that when it comes to sizing, these sweats have a “mega” fit, which means they’re oversized. I still sized up just to make sure mine would be roomy, but learned that I didn’t need to. These give you an oversized fit at your true size. Plus, as a shorter girlie (5’2!), I was thrilled that they came in short, regular, and long lengths. They’re still just the tiniest bit long, so I flip the elastic on each ankle under to shorten the legs. You can’t tell a thing!

Set Active Staple SET Uniform Layered Crewneck.

Set Active Staple Straight Leg Sweatpants.

This vintage-inspired sweatsuit from Set Active is made from 100% cotton, for those who want to prioritize more natural fibers. “I love how soft they feel,” Hsieh notes. “Sometimes 100% cotton feels stiff to me, and I’ve found that cotton sweats in particular lay weirdly at the chest when they’re oversized, but these maintain their plushy softness.”.

It has been revealed that this set is mid-weight, cozy, and warm. “I love a crewneck and sweatpants to sleep in, but sometimes find other sweats to be too much underneath my many layers of comforter and other blankets. These are the perfect weight to be warm and let me sleep comfortably,” Hsieh says. The crewneck isn't too bulky either—a challenge for a lot of sweatshirts—and fits easily underneath a jacket.

This set comes in tons of bold colorways, with contrasting collars and retro logos on the crewneck—so it’s great for anybody who's into the vintage activewear look. The only con? Hsieh, who is 5’3, found that pants run slightly long.

lululemon Scuba Oversized Full-Zip Hoodie.

lululemon Scuba Mid-Rise Wide-Leg Pant.

This lululemon hoodie was named the best zip-up in our guide to the best hoodies for its comfy, classic fit. Where the hoodie shines, according to Associate Style & Commerce Editor Shannen Zitz, the pants are just as impressive. Both stand out for the waffle material: A soft, stretchy blend of cotton, modal, and polyester. She finds it more breathable than some of her buttery-smooth cotton sweats. Another perk? It’s basically immune to pilling.

According to recent reports, “Both pieces are incredibly soft and cozy,” Zitz indicates. “I love the slightly oversized, waist-length fit of the top. It pairs really well with the matching sweatpants, which are equally comfy and have a flattering drape with a straight-leg fit.”.

Sources indicate that this set styled with a plain white tee underneath and a pair of comfortable sneakers “happens to be my travel fit of choice,” she notes. “The hoodie keeps me warm and cozy during cold flights and early morning departure days, but I can easily unzip it or tie it around my waist if I get too warm.”.

Vuori Restore Straight Leg Sweatpant.

The Restore hoodie is one of Vuori’s best sellers, and for good reason. “I love the material,” Richey claims. “It’s very soft and feels super durable.” The French terry material (a cotton blend that’s smooth on the outside with brushed fleece on the inside)is made of breathable cotton and sturdy polyester.

In a recent development, as far as sweat sets go, this one has a lot of heft. The Restore line is thicker and denser than the label's BlissBlend or DreamKnit lines, making this set incredibly warm with a high-quality, structured feel. “The softness seems to also stay wash after wash, which is a huge win!” Richey adds.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to fit, the hoodie has a perfectly oversized shape, but you might benefit from sizing up in the bottoms, particularly if you’re thicker-thighed, Ritchey notes. The pant comes in short, regular, and long lengths, giving you even more options to find the right fit.

This Spanx set stands out as a lighter-weight and more polished option. “This set feels so light and airy,” claims Zitz. Spanx’s Air Essentials is made of their signature Spacer Fabric (a blend of modal, polyester, and elastane), for an ultra-smooth feel with plenty of stretch.

Industry observers note that “It’s one of the most comfortable lounge sets I own, but also one of the nicest looking,” Zitz says. The structured half-zip top and tailored (yet roomy) wide-leg pant have an almost dressed-up look, so you can wear the set to lounge or out of the house. It also comes in nearly 20 colors—a range of neutrals to bright options like red, blue, and plum.

There is one downside: Neither the top nor bottom has pockets. While they might take away from the streamlined look, being able to slip your phone or wallet into a small pocket would be a bonus.

Gap VintageSoft Oversized Henley Pullover.

Gap VintageSoft Baggy Wide-Leg Sweatpants.

Gap certainly holds its own in the loungewear category. Aside from the cozy feel (thanks to a blend of cotton and polyester), it really shines when it comes to style.

Sources indicate that “I love a wide-leg sweatpant,” Zitz says. “I find they look less loungey than a jogger, and this pair is roomy without swallowing up my entire frame.” Even better is the henley top: The button-up design and mock neck make this top look more chic than your average crewneck or half-zip. “It’s unlike any other sweatshirt I own in terms of style,” Zitz says.

It has been revealed that one area for improvement: The color options. Our tester opted for a soft blue color, but would have preferred a more neutral gray—it just wasn’t in stock due to the limited colorways.

Rhone DreamGlow Barrel Leg Pant.

It has been revealed that rhone is another label that the WH fitness and style editors love. I have personally been a fan of their DreamGlow line for a while. It’s warm, but also has a sleek feel to it. There’s no heaviness to this set at all.

Made primarily of polyester and a small amount of elastane, the fabric also contains lyocell, a semi-synthetic fiber that helps to wick moisture away from the body, creating a slightly cooling effect. This set is ideal for anyone who runs hot or for transitional spring or fall weather. I like to wear it around my apartment on work-from-home days or as a travel outfit.

This is also the set for someone who is a little sweatsuit-reluctant. The top has a slightly cropped and boxy fit, while the pants are a barrel-leg shape (a.k.a. a flared mid-leg and tapered ankle). Combined with the ultra-smooth material, this set looks less frumpy than your old-school sweat suits.

The portfolio risk Toobit’s growth chief wants AI to flag before a trade

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Holding a basket of different tokens often feels like diversification, right up until a market downturn drags them all down at once.
  • Toobit’s chief growth officer, Yasser Elmansy, told CryptoSlate he’d like an AI assistant to warn traders when a fresh position adds to a risk they already carry.
  • For Elmansy, the goal isn’t to hand trading over to bots, but to give retail owners better visibility before they click buy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Holding a basket of different tokens often feels like diversification, right up until a market downturn drags them all down at once.

Toobit’s chief growth officer, Yasser Elmansy, told CryptoSlate he’d like an AI assistant to warn traders when a fresh position adds to a risk they already carry.

For Elmansy, the goal isn’t to hand trading over to bots, but to give retail owners better visibility before they click buy.

Trading once required a phone call to a broker; the internet moved it to computers, and smartphones put market access in people’s pockets.

“The internet changed how we execute decisions; AI could change how we prepare for and make them,” he indicates.

Elmansy imagines an assistant that, with a trader’s permission, could review holdings, open positions, leverage, and trading history. Suppose the trader owns several tokens that tend to move together. The assistant could explain how a single downturn might affect all those positions and how leverage can magnify a loss.

The trader would still set objectives and risk limits, authorize access, and approve consequential actions.

“I’d rather see AI help someone make a better-informed decision than simply push them to trade more.”.

Models can misread information or produce convincing but wrong explanations, he warns, and in a leveraged market, small errors can be costly. If many automated strategies react to the same signals, they can worsen volatility.

“Speed isn’t always an advantage if everyone responds in the same way,” he says.

He wants leverage controls and clear ways to pause or stop automation.

In a recent development, that emphasis on informed participation carries over into how Elmansy approaches growth at Toobit. He helps choose partners among trading communities and creators and discusses deal terms. Rather than chasing raw follower counts, he looks at how many people actively trade, how long they stay involved, and how much trading takes place.

He says Toobit already uses those criteria to assess prospective partners.

“I don’t want to attach a specific growth figure to that work without verified reporting,” he says.

The chief growth officer role is recent, he claims, so he “wouldn’t claim to have transformed the business in that capacity already.” What has changed is the scope of his thinking.

“To me, sustainable growth isn’t only about why users arrive; it’s also about why they stay,” he adds.

Elmansy’s focus on building durable systems and questioning standard playbooks comes from two decades of learning business and crypto from the ground up.

His first venture started in sixth grade, when he told his brother and a relative he was working in advertising and both asked to join.

“Rather than admitting I didn’t actually have a business, I decided to give them an assignment,” he states.

Industry observers note that armed with a print catalog from a shop his father’s accounting firm used, Elmansy learned that 100 business cards cost about three pounds to produce. He sent his recruits to nearby businesses, including a supermarket, to sell them for 20 pounds.

“To my complete surprise, they both came back with customers and money,” he recalls.

In a recent development, he placed the orders, delivered the cards, and started again. Websites and Facebook ads followed. For years he found the clients and did the work himself, until the business hit a wall because he couldn't scale alone. He convinced a backer to help fund an office and staff, and rolled out his first marketing agency in 2013, concluding that growth eventually requires trusting people and building structure.

He remembers keeping pictures of Bill Gates and Mark Zuckerberg on that first office wall. He wanted to build his own technology organization.

“I wasn’t interested in technology simply as a tool for marketing,” he indicates.

Industry observers note that by 2019, the agency had around 40 employees. When the pandemic hit, businesses cut marketing budgets, so he scaled back and spent late 2020 studying decentralized exchanges and liquidity pools.

Recent findings suggest that after watching an OKX webinar, he contacted the exchange’s recruitment team. He lacked the business development background it wanted, but pitched his marketing and DeFi knowledge and got a chance.

When he joined, his manager mentioned a trading-volume target of $100,000.

“I genuinely didn’t know whether that was large or small,” he says.

Sources indicate that what Elmansy did know was influencer marketing. At OKX, he says, he challenged assumptions about what the exchange should pay its partners and argued for backing deals he believed in. He spent nearly three and a half years at OKX, then worked at Pionex, before he joined Toobit in January 2026 as head of global business development.

Industry observers note that looking ahead, Elmansy thinks crypto will reach more people when sending money gets simpler. Today, he states, users still have to think about wallets, private keys, networks, and fees “before they can do something as basic as moving value.” He wants users to understand the risks they take even as the mechanics get easier.

Disclosure: This is a sponsored interview, paid for by Toobit. CryptoSlate interviewed Yasser Elmansy, Toobit’s chief growth officer, and all quotes come from that interview. This article is not investment advice. Crypto trading, especially with leverage, carries a risk of loss.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A Tesla Model Y left a parkway in El Dorado Hills, California, hit a tree and burst into flames in September, killing three of the four people inside.
  • It has been revealed that the crash was widely covered in the Sacramento area as a fiery single-car wreck.
  • In a recent development, late on Saturday, September 12, 2026, a 2024 Tesla Model Y with four people inside was heading west on Serrano Parkway, between Terracina Drive and Silva Valley Parkway.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A Tesla Model Y left a parkway in El Dorado Hills, California, hit a tree and burst into flames in September, killing three of the four people inside. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators states Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, with the car doing 74 mph.

It has been revealed that the crash was widely covered in the Sacramento area as a fiery single-car wreck. None of that coverage mentioned a driver-assist system. It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data.

In a recent development, late on Saturday, September 12, 2026, a 2024 Tesla Model Y with four people inside was heading west on Serrano Parkway, between Terracina Drive and Silva Valley Parkway. That’s a residential part of the Serrano community in El Dorado Hills, east of Sacramento.

According to the CHP’s Placerville office, the Model Y left the road “for unknown reasons,” hit a tree on the north side of the parkway, and caught fire. Officers got the call around 10:38 p.m. By the time they arrived, the car was fully engulfed in flames.

Charles Anthony Cameron, 30, of Sacramento, was thrown from the car and died at the scene. Alejandra Mendoza, 28, of Sacramento, and Kailauna Viola Mills, 28, of Roseville, were found dead inside once firefighters put out the fire. One of the two women was driving; CHP hasn’t publicly mentioned which.

Mills lived in Arizona and was visiting family. Her uncle told CBS Sacramento she worked in the medical field and was supposed to get married next April.

A fourth person, a 28-year-old Sacramento woman, survived with major injuries.

Recent findings suggest that CHP says the cause is still under investigation. Speed, impairment, and how the car left the road haven’t been released. And nobody has said a word about Autopilot.

Under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone is killed or hurt. Tesla filed a report on this one.

Sources indicate that it lists a 2024 Model Y, a consumer vehicle, and marks the “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged.” That’s Tesla confirming through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 74 mph, a fatality, and the California Highway Patrol as the investigating agency.

Then it redacts the narrative, the software version, and whether the road was inside the system’s operating domain, all as “confidential business information,” the same treatment Tesla gives 99.9% of its reports.

According to recent reports, the rest of the report is strangely thin. Tesla lists the roadway type as “Unknown” and what the car hit as “Unknown,” even though police stated it was a tree. It checks only one source for how it learned of the crash: the media. So Tesla found out about a triple-fatal crash in one of its cars from the news, then went into its own data and confirmed its driver-assist was on.

How we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 05:36 UTC, which is 10:36 p.m. Pacific on September 12, within two minutes of the 10:38 p.m. call CHP responded to. The city, the 2024 Model Y, the month, and the fatal outcome all line up. It’s the only fatal Tesla driver-assist report from El Dorado Hills in the data. It’s the same crash.

Two of the three victims were found inside the car after the fire was out. The survivor got out of, or was pulled from, the wreckage, depending on the report.

It has been revealed that CHP hasn’t said whether the doors played any role, and we’re not suggesting they did. But it’s a fair question to ask about any Tesla crash with a fire, now that NHTSA is writing new rules for emergency door releases after years of complaints about people getting trapped. We’ve asked.

Industry observers note that this is the second triple-fatal crash in Tesla’s latest NHTSA filings where its driver-assist was verified engaged and the public never heard about it. The other one was on I-75 in Naples. Add Vineland and July’s four fatal crashes, and the pattern is hard to miss.

"what little effort went into the report"?

I disagree, a lot of effort went in to minimize the report, to portray it as an unremarkable accident.

That is the effort I find Tesla criminally responsible for.

Recent findings suggest that the CHP need the full report, no redactions. If they chose to censor it that is their task, not Tesla's.

What stands out in this one is how little effort went into the report. Tesla knows the speed, knows the system was on, and has telematics. But it couldn’t fill in what the car hit, and it learned about three deaths in one of its cars from the news. Then it redacted the one field, the narrative, that would tell us what the car did.

Tesla wants regulators and customers to trust FSD with no one watching. That trust has to be earned with data. A company that seals the account of what its car did at 74 mph in a neighborhood, in a crash that killed three people, isn’t earning it.

It has been revealed that we’re asking CHP Placerville whether its investigators knew the system was engaged, whether they got Tesla’s raw data or Tesla’s summary of it, and what they found about the fire and the doors. If CHP never got the full data, how will it ever determine the cause?

Home » Blitz news » Latest EU Crypto Sanctions Extend SWIFT’s Russia Blockade.

The Commission just granted a multi-faceted sanction package going ham on Russia’s various uses of crypto.

The European Commission’s 22nd sanctions package against Russia extends the European Union’s (EU) transaction ban to over 60 Russian banks and indicates all 60 of those will be removed from SWIFT, President Ursula von der Leyen stated in Strasbourg on 23 November 2026.

According to recent reports, this comes just weeks after Russia officially legalized crypto currency trading, starting with the massive-cap coins like Bitcoin (BTC) & Ethereum (ETH). In the 22nd sanction packet, Russian-linked crypto services & platforms were specifically named as banned for transactions.

In a recent development, “The measures include the possibility for EU firms to sue their non-Russian contractual parties in the EU to recover damages.”, – states the document. “We will continue to propose new sanctions until Russia demonstrates genuine intent for a lasting peace in Ukraine”, further said the Chief Commissioner.

With this package, we are increasing the pressure.We are striking harder at Russia’s ways to finance its war, by targeting its banks and crypto platforms.We are further isolating Russia. We are shutting the door to its participation to European sports and cultural events.… pic.twitter.com/9Ltkpohylq.

While focusing on Russian SWIFT sanctions, the EU added 51 entities to the anti-circumvention list, while the majority of them, 27, were outside Russia: 14 came from China, including four in Hong Kong, four in Türkiye, three in Kyrgyzstan, two in India, two in Kazakhstan and two more in the United Arab Emirates (UAE).

The European Union (EU) freshly assembled the Crypto Task Force to counter new crypto-related ways of evading the huge pile of sanctions, including limitations of Russian business abroad via ‘third-world’ parties. The Council will decide when the ban enters into force, after the necessary measures are activated.

  • IN A WORLD where home workout trends change with the seasons, the exercise bike continues to stand the test of time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

IN A WORLD where home workout trends change with the seasons, the exercise bike continues to stand the test of time. Its appeal lies in its ability to increase cardiovascular health through a low-impact approach, with limitless ability to take it up a notch. With a range of indoor exercise bike styles available, from air bikes to spin bikes and even recumbent bikes, it can be difficult to choose the right style for your fitness goals and preferences.

Recent innovations in "smart" bikes have expanded the indoor bike market even further, offering a wider selection than ever before. So we leveraged the extensive collective experience of MH fitness editors, anchored by months of hands-on testing from certified trainers, to distinguish which factors set the top options apart from the rest.

In a recent development, each of the bikes in this guide can help people burn calories and improve overall fitness, but certain styles diverge in fundamental ways. Spin bikes, similar to what you might find at a SoulCycle class, engage your core and legs, while air bikes require you to use your upper body as well. Air bike enthusiasts appreciate their effectiveness in high-intensity interval training and circuit-style workouts due to their ability to require quick bursts of intense effort. Meanwhile, spin bikes cater to a broader range of intensities, longer cycling sessions, and supplementing outdoor cycling routines.

Sources indicate that to help you select the ideal exercise bike for you and your home gym, we've curated a list of the top exercise bikes we've personally tested, fitting all budget levels. From the ultra-high-end Peloton Bike+ to the most budget-friendly options available on Amazon, we've got you covered. Continue scrolling to discover the seven best exercise bikes, according to fitness editors and certified trainers, but first, a few things to keep in mind.

It has been revealed that being the Fitness and Reviews Editor of Men's Health means I get my hands on every piece of upcoming gym gear that releases, sometimes before it's available to the public. To build this guide of the best exercise bikes, I took stock of the bestselling bikes on the market and put them up against overlooked classics and newly released options. I used each of these bikes for months, during long rides, interval training, as a warm-up, or a workout finisher.

Over the years, Men's Health editors like fitness director Ebenezer Samuel, CSCS, as well as key fitness trainers from both the MH Advisory Board and the MH Strength in Diversity Initiative, have taken great care in researching and evaluating the wide pool of exercise bikes. Their insights were also integral in creating this list. Our team also enlisted the help of Maillard Howell of Dean CrossFit in Brooklyn to test and assess how well these bikes performed in a real-world scenario (read: a high-volume, high-traffic training facility).

Ultimately, we ended up with the below guide that represents our top picks for the best exercise bikes we recommend buying now.

In a recent development, this new REP Fitness bike is one of the most impressive air bikes that our Fitness Director, Ebenezer Samuel, CSCS, has ever used. “The eight damper settings create a ton of options for my training,” he states. “And they essentially let the Strive simulate just about any air bike on the market.”.

In a recent development, this Variable Pitch Resistance (VPR) system allows you to change the angle of the fan blades to give you that additional control over your workout. Most of us recognize the air bike for its impressive ability to make you suffer more the harder that you pedal it.

But with this new system, the Strive bike gives you the ability to use it for steady-state and recovery rides as well as those brutal finisher and max-effort sessions.

In a recent development, “At an 8, this feels like a serious strength-style quad-pump that's harder per pedal than a Rogue Echo or Scwhinn Airdyne,” says Samuel. “That versatility, and the speed with which you can switch between settings, opens a newly introduced world of fan bike workouts.”.

The Strive is also as sturdy as they come among fanbikes. Underrated: The cupholder is everything you want on a bike, suitable for small plastic bottles and larger metal jugs alike (and great for your iPhone too).

Read more: How Our Fitness Director Overhauled His Garage Gym.

Industry observers note that this bike is no slouch when it comes to its hardware. In fact, it offers many of the same features as bikes double its price. From adjustable handlebars to convenient dumbbell holders, 32 levels of resistance, toe-cage pedals, and a spacious touchscreen display, it boasts all the features you'd expect from a premium bike. And it's wrapped in a sleek, matte black finish that oozes style.

The assembly is fairly easy, taking about 45 minutes to set up. The bike arrives in a box about 85 percent built with just the feet, handles, and pedals needing to be mounted. The bike has a nice compact frame and takes up the least amount of space in the home. The brand found a way to cut down on the cost by removing the expensive touchscreen and giving you a platform to place your own mobile device or tablet on, allowing you to follow any classes you want that way.

Whether we were sprinting or climbing out of the saddle during intense workouts, this bike offered unwavering stability. We never found ourselves wobbling or feeling uneasy on this machine. The elevated bullhorn handlebars aren’t just about style; they provide an elbow rest that we found essential during grueling climbs. It's a thoughtful touch that we found enhances overall riding comfort. The competition-style seat on this bike strikes a balance between comfort and support that other bikes we've tested in this price range miss the mark on. It's designed for long sessions, providing that Goldilocks level of cushioning.

This bike offers an all-around fantastic workout experience, especially for the cost, and is a great pick no matter your goals.

Read More: Best Workout Clothes, Tested by Us.

The NordicTrack X24 earned its spot here because it doesn't just deliver cutting-edge training technology to the user, it also delivers the world for those more adventure-minded riders.

Do you want to feel like you are cycling through the Swiss Alps or along the beaches of Hawaii? That's what the NordicTrack offers, and not just by showing pretty landscapes on its 22-inch screen. Unlike the other bikes in this guide that simulate incline and decline by adjusting the magnetic resistance, this one actually replicates climbs or descents for a more accurate feeling of winding up and down the hills of Switzerland.

The setup is easy enough to do solo, but it helps if you have a person around to help you for some of the more involved moments of assembly. The bike is sturdy and robust, but also heavy, weighing over 200 pounds. So be sure that you build it in close proximity to where you are going to want to ride it, because it's not very easy to move around.

Like most NordicTrack equipment, the X24 comes with a year-long iFit membership.

Read More: Best Under Desk Bikes, Tested by Us.

It has been revealed that looking for a bike that can handle years of punishment? Well, if the end of the world comes knocking, the Rogue Echo Bike will likely still be pedaling away. This thing is solid as a rock, capable of handling whatever you throw its way. This bike is a strength builder and a monster maker, demanding legit power from the user to make it move.

In a recent development, the bike arrives at your door well-packaged and about 80 percent assembled. The screen, arms, pedals, and feet are all that you need to mount. The process can take about an hour to get your bike ready to ride.

Industry observers note that its belt drive system is consistent and essentially maintenance-free, meaning you can focus on your workout, not tinkering around with the machine. We've used this bike on and off for more than seven years and have never experienced technical issues.

Recent findings suggest that beyond its durability, this bike rides like a dream. Pedaling is smooth and fluid in motion, and returns more resistance in response to the rider's effort.

It has been revealed that we don't just recommend this bike; we swear by it. Years of firsthand testing have made it abundantly clear that if air bikes had Oscars, this one would be walking away with the golden statue, no doubt.Another unique feature of the Rogue Echo Bike is its fan blades. They’re crafted from thin-gauge steel, cut out and treated to a powder coating and welded to a central hub within the fan cage. While this level of detail might seem unnecessary, it adds to the fan's long-term reliability and overall aesthetic.

Now, we won't sugarcoat it; this machine is heavy. But fear not, because it comes equipped with wheels at the front. So, even if you're not the Hulk, you can still shuffle it around to ensure it fits in your workout space.

The only other qualm we have with this bike is that it doesn't feature multi-grip handles like other air bike models do.

Read More: Best Rowing Machines.

There's a reason that Peloton's bikes have remained popular through the highs and lows of at-home training. The brand combines a superbly designed, connected bike with a charismatic crew of trainers and has ignited a fitness following.

Industry observers note that the delivery is taken care of by Peloton, which unboxes and mounts the bike for you at your chosen location—an example of the high level of service that comes from the brand. The bike itself is fairly durable, and relatively simplistic outside of the 21.5-inch HD touchscreen. If you are interested in also utilizing the strength classes, consider Peloton's Cross Training Bike+, which comes with a pair of dumbbells and additional amenities like built-in Sonos speakers.

The truth is, when you buy a Peloton you are buying more than a bike, you are buying a community. And you are getting a best-in-class library of instructor-led, studio-style classes. From cycling to off-bike sessions like core workouts and hybrid strength classes, the variety of content is endless. The engaging live class offerings and fun gamification of your data makes the bike especially great for beginners or anyone who has difficulty maintaining a regimen.

Sources indicate that on the downside, the initial investment can be a detractor, and the monthly subscription fee for access to Peloton's classes can also add up ($49.99 a month for all-access). However, if you fully utilize the platform and its library of classes, it can be a worthwhile expense.

Sources indicate that the only other glitch that our team had was instead of a traditional foot cage, the Peloton requires Delta-compatible cleats (which you can buy here) that clip into the pedals. It’s another step, and another purchase, before you start your ride. But this is to allow for the best experience with the programmed classes and resistance level changes, so it's an understandable ask. Peloton also offers a 30-day in-home trial with free delivery, setup, and, if needed, pickup and return for a small fee of $150. It's a commitment to customer satisfaction that helps protect your investment in this bike.

What we like about the Schwinn Fitness 290 Recumbent Bike is its excellent value. Sure, it doesn't have an overly huge touchscreen display, but that means you aren't tricked into spending your money on a bunch of technology you don't need. Plus, you can place your phone, tablet, or other device on the media shelf so you can ride along to on-demand, trainer-led classes with real-time coaching.

The seat's padding provides a lot of cushioning and ventilation, meaning you won't want to cut your workout short because you're uncomfortable. The weighted strapped pedals are also a win, because they feel secure on your feet so you can focus on your ride and not whether you’re going to lose traction.

The relatively lightweight build of this bike is also a positive, as anyone who has shopped for a recumbent bike understands. The majority of models are built like tanks, making them very hard to move around the house. The 290 also comes with rollers, making it even easier to transport.

How well this is built should be no surprise considering how long Schwinn has been in the bike game. This model is extremely comfortable for most sizes, including taller individuals, which is a nice improvement from the previous 230 version.

Read More: The Best Recumbent Bikes, Tested by Us.

We understand that some of the bikes in this guide might be a little expensive for beginners who aren’t certain if they can stick with a new cardio routine or don’t need something that can handle intense workouts.

In a recent development, merach is a brand that we’ve tested decent products from, and other pieces of its equipment have made our guides in the past. This design won’t take up much space, and it offers a good range of intensity through magnetic resistance.

Now, if you’re looking for an exercise bike that is going to take a lot of punishment and will handle whatever you throw at it, you might want to consider one of the more serious models above. This ride is only 62 pounds, which absolutely puts it on the lighter side and therefore prone to a little less stability if you’re really jamming on it.

According to recent reports, if you’re looking for an easy-to-use bike from a trusted manufacturer, this is your best play for the money. And customers on Amazon have commented on how quiet it is, with Merach putting it under 25 decibels in use.

Recent findings suggest that in general, both devices can work for both high-intensity interval training workouts and long cardio. But how you prioritize your training will determine which bike is best for you. If you plan to focus on HIIT-based workouts, or want to mix weight training and bodyweight in with your bike work, the air bike is your jam. It’s easier to dismount the bike after a one-minute interval, then do a set of pushups, for example, making this ideal if you love CrossFit-style training.

If those steady-state workouts are your focus or you're using an indoor exercise bike to supplement outdoor riding, hop on a spin bike and get ready to pedal. And if you like doing cardio while watching TV, also opt for the spin bike; fan bikes are incredibly loud.

Everyone has different fitness levels and goals, but not every bike can cater to these needs. Look for a bike with adjustable resistance levels, allowing you to customize the intensity of your workouts however you choose. This is especially notable if you're planning to evolve the intensity of your workouts in the coming months and years.

In a recent development, magnetic resistance is often the smoothest, most predictable option, which is what you can find in most spin bikes. This allows bike makers like Peloton to seamlessly integrate the resistance level with its online classes. While air bike options like Rogue and Assault use traditional methods of wheel fans and friction to challenge your endurance.

It has been revealed that the display should be easy to use and show all the essentials, including speed, distance, and time. Extra features like a heart rate monitor, Bluetooth connectivity, and USB ports can be nice to have, so decide if any of those are dealbreakers for you. For the higher-end spin bikes, the screens are more like full-service entertainment centers that can be used to watch a class with your favorite trainer or take you through a great cycling route in the Alps.

According to recent reports, some exercise bikes include preset workout programs, while others may offer a membership-based training app. Consider if having built-in programs is important to you, and if it is, if you want to consider a membership that would allow for a greater library of programs. There is typically a cost involved, so if you proposal on using those features, be sure to confirm whether or not they are included. In some cases, these bikes might work perfectly without those higher-level subscriptions.

Consider the dimensions of the bikes you're shopping for, especially if you have limited space. Some bikes come with compact designs and foldable options for easier storage. If you'll need to stow the bike away when not in use, look for a lightweight frame on wheels.

Because exercise bikes are such a substantial investment, budget and warranty go hand-in-hand. Many of the bike models we recommend offer a solid warranty of between one and seven years on parts, plus at least a one-year warranty on labor. This is totally reasonable, especially if you're spending north of $1,500 on a upcoming machine. You should expect that your bike's frame and resistance mechanism should both be warrantied for the life of the unit.

A 2019 study showed that regular use of an exercise bike—alone or combined with strength training—can have a positive impact on aerobic capacity in as little as three months. Researchers also concluded that, like other forms of regular cardio, using an exercise bike can also contribute to a reduction in systolic and diastolic blood pressure—especially when combined with a heart-healthy diet.

Industry observers note that indoor cycling is also a low-impact form of cardio, resulting in less pressure on the joints than activities like running or jumping. Cycling is not a load-bearing exercise, indicates Kate Heelan, PhD, a Professor of Research at the University of Nebraska at Kearney. This helps to minimize the risk of injury caused by malalignment, loss of balance, etc.

It's hard to beat the fresh air and sense of freedom an outdoor ride offers, but indoor cycling has a few unique benefits that can't be duplicated on the road. It starts with the fact you can hit hills or flat road when and how you want, just with the press of a button.

Because you'll never quite be 'coasting' or riding downhill on an exercise bike, indoor cycling workouts can allow you to get the benefit of several hours’ worth of outdoor riding done in half the time.

In a recent development, cycling is an amazing way to get in shape and stay healthy, there's no doubt about it. But when it comes to choosing between indoor and outdoor cycling, what are the real differences?

"Broadly, both devices will burn calories and offer cardiovascular benefit," indicates MH fitness director Ebenezer Samuel, CSCS, "But they’re not the same experience.".

For starters, there's the convenience factor. Indoor cycling is ideal for those who are short on time or live in regions where the terrain or weather may limit getting a ride outdoors. It can be much easier to hop on an indoor bike at home or at the gym and get a great workout without having to worry about traffic, the environment, or safety concerns.

Both modalities lead to cardiovascular benefits and, like any activity, they both burn calories. But outdoor cycling challenges other qualities, says Samuel. "You’re actively moving through space when you cycle outdoors," says Samuel, "which challenges your muscles to decelerate, react, and constantly micro-correct in ways it won’t on a stationary bike." The outdoor bike also offers a basic balance challenge that the indoor bike lacks.

Outdoors, the terrain and your pace set the challenge. Indoors, however, you can more easily customize your intensity, simply adjusting the resistance level on your bike. This (and the removal of the balance challenge) can make indoor cycling more beginner-friendly.

Many indoor bikes offer an interactive component now, like instructor-led classes and competitive leaderboards, which can be a great way to stay motivated and challenge yourself. These classes also provide a sense of community and support to stay motivated and hungry, even when you're working out alone.

Recent findings suggest that exercise bikes are generally considered to be a low-impact form of exercise, and they're a joint-friendly way to burn calories. But it's still vital to take precautions to avoid the potential of injury. Here are some tips to help you stay safe on an exercise bike:.

Charles Thorp is the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, where he shares the best product recommendations in gym equipment, recovery tools, supplements, and more. Following an early life in athletics, Charles became a NASM-certified trainer and began writing programs alongside the most respected coaches in the world. #133192. Latest Update: The 10 Best Fitness Trackers, Tested by Our Fitness and Tech Experts

📅 15 Mar 2024 • ⏱️ 22m • 📚 Deep Dive (4322 w)
