⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Set in a wide Brooklyn Heights brownstone, photographer Ethan James Green’s apartment, though modest in scale, gives the impression of a breakfast room in some well-appointed Cornish estate.
  • Paintings by Raphael Soyer flank a portrait by Thomas Hart Benton in the living room; armchairs by George Mann Niedecken.
  • Recent findings suggest that just under 1,000 square feet, the one-bedroom unit serves dual purposes: to provide space to converge with his cherished friends and to house other faces that inspire him.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Set in a wide Brooklyn Heights brownstone, photographer Ethan James Green’s apartment, though modest in scale, gives the impression of a breakfast room in some well-appointed Cornish estate. Hulking Victorian, Arts and Crafts, and Jacobean furniture dominates the space, Art Nouveau lamps aglow. The home draws an interesting contrast to the work for which he is best known—whether his black-and-white shoot with Kate Moss for Dazed or his recent Vanity Fair cover story with Carlos Alcaraz. Green’s apartment is, by comparison, more indicative of a bygone era, but it still reflects the irreverent, empathetic spirit at the heart of his practice.

The view from the bedroom into the living room.

Paintings by Raphael Soyer flank a portrait by Thomas Hart Benton in the living room; armchairs by George Mann Niedecken.

Recent findings suggest that just under 1,000 square feet, the one-bedroom unit serves dual purposes: to provide space to converge with his cherished friends and to house other faces that inspire him. Covering walls are the many 20th-century figurative paintings Green has gathered over the years, among them Social Realist portraits by Raphael Soyer, nudes both bold and tentative, and myriad depictions of introspective souls—images that captured Green in a spiritual grip.

Recent findings suggest that he displays the varied mix in interiors conceived with his friend Dylan Bailey, the New York–based artist and set designer, whom he met years ago on a shoot. Their collaboration was informal. Green would come home and find paint swatches left by Bailey, who might pop by and hang up a work while Green was shooting. The furniture they found at auction. “I wanted to have matching couches so when a friend comes over we can both take one, sink in, and talk,” states Green. The vintage sofas’ peach upholstery fits right in. “I didn’t realize until after getting them that the color showed up in several of the paintings,” Green says, referring to a portrait of an ironworker by Joseph Paul Vorst and a double nude by George Valentine Dureau.

A Victorian Renaissance Revival bed mingles with works by Maurice Grosser, Raphael Soyer, and Moses Soyer.

Green in the kitchen, surrounded by photographs.

Green grew up outside Grand Rapids, Michigan, surrounded by, as he recalls, “cornfields and dairy farms.” With missionary parents, unstructured days, and endless skies, he had the space and time to imagine a different life. “I knew I wanted to be a fashion photographer when I was 14 or 15, then found out I could model at 16,” he recalls. “I won the lottery. Modeling was a better way to learn than art school.” He moved to Fresh York City at 17, the first student to graduate from his high school online. “I had to be here,” he states simply. “My first year in New York I shot with David Armstrong. He took me under his wing.”.

Recent findings suggest that now in his mid-30s, Green splits his time between the Big Apple and Los Angeles with his boyfriend. On the East Coast, between shoots, he runs Latest York Life Gallery, opened in 2022 and named after the Chinatown insurance company across the street. His first show, dedicated to Baltimore-based photographer Steven Cuffie’s tender portraits of Black women, reflected Green’s devotion to his own medium and enduring interest in the variance of human faces. The 2023 exhibition “Sleeping Beauties” would blur the lines between Green’s life and work: Many of the paintings shown have come to reside in his apartment.

Green kneels before a bookshelf by Renzo Mongiardino in the bedroom, which is painted in a custom Benjamin Moore blue.

It has been revealed that portraits by Raphael Soyer and Leroy E. Mitchell Jr. flank The bedroom’s 19th-century French armoire, which reflects a view of another Soyer painting.

An Austrian Art Nouveau chandelier hangs in the living room, which displays paintings by (from left) Raphael Soyer, Joseph Paul Vorst, Raphael Soyer, and Hermann Grom-Rottmayer. The walls are painted in a custom Benjamin Moore color.

A 1949 self-portrait by Leroy E. Mitchell Jr., for instance, hangs in the bedroom. This was the first painting Green bought at auction, prior to which it had been found in a dumpster. Green’s research led him to Mitchell’s early life in Detroit, his community of peers, and his time as a teacher in Ghana. Meanwhile, one of Green’s most pedigreed finds, a painting by Thomas Hart Benton, whose 1931 mural of industrial workers hangs in The Met, stoked another uncovering. “I had gotten multiple paintings and then realized many of the artists knew each other or were friends,” he states, noting that Benton and Vorst were studio mates. It is like Green is uncovering a parallel life of creatives finding true kinship.

In a recent development, green Crowned the kitchen cabinet with art, including works by Raphael Soyer, Robert Philipp, and David Armstrong. To its right hang photographs by (from top) Nan Goldin, David Armstrong, and Richard Avedon.

Framed family snapshots fill the hallway shelves.

It is these serendipitous journeys into the lives of other artists that Green cherishes as much as the art itself. “I love paintings,” he says. Perhaps a bit too much? Bailey would tease him that every time he arrived there was yet another portrait to place. “The reason there’s one hanging on the mirror over the mantel is because I had no more wall space,” Green says. As he explains, his collection, like his life and work, is ultimately about affection. “You cannot be a good photographer without being empathetic,” Green observes. “I love people. I love faces.” He’s made sure that love is hard to miss.

The VW ID. Polo Trend with the 37 kWh battery went on sale in Europe in July, starting at just 24,995 euros, or about $27,500, with a WLTP range of 207 miles (334 km).

By mid-September, reports claimed Volkswagen’s entry-level EV was already essentially sold out across actross all trims, with more than 30,000 orders and a 10-month waitlist.

According to the latest enhancement from German automotive news outlet Edison Media, that number has doubled in about two months, and buyers now face delivery times of up to 21 months for the base ID. Polo Trend. Deliveries for the sporty GTI version are expected to be around seven months.

Industry observers note that “We clearly planned too conservatively,” a VW manager told Edison during an interview. While VW expected about 90 to 95% to choose to lease, the leasing rate is only about 50%.

The larger 52 kWh battery version has also seen higher-than-expected demand, while 90% surprisingly opted to buy the optional €810 ($890) detachable towbar.

The 52 kWh battery version will go on sale in the UK this week, starting at £30,260 ($40,000). The ID. Cross Life with the 37 kWh battery will go on sale in January 2027, starting at £26,985 ($35,500).

Industry observers note that volkswagen’s new entry-level electric cars are off to a promising start. The electric urban car family, which includes the ID. Polo, ID. Cross, and the CUPRA Raval and Skoda Epiq, has received nearly 150,000 orders combined since production began in June.

Sources indicate that however, the German automaker is still facing an uphill battle. The VW Group posted an operating loss of 5.9 billion euros ($6.5 billion) in the third quarter, its worst quarterly loss since the Dieselgate scandal.

In September, Volkswagen’s supervisory board approved its Future Plan 2030, which calls for reducing its global workforce by up to 100,000, closing plants, and narrowing its vehicle lineup to cut costs.

According to recent reports, whether you equate The North Face with everyday city wear or outdoor adventures, it’s a solid, time-tested spot to get a gift for a loved one (or yourself). The brand has jackets and accessories with familiar winter looks, as well as products with less expected silhouettes that still offer protection from the elements in an understated style.

Here’s a look at some of the best cold-weather gear that will have you wrapping up the gift of warmth and durability… even if that gift is for yourself.

This is an easy gifting win because the warm, hooded, insulated jacket is a recognizable The North Face staple, evoking an unpretentious spin on the brand’s iconic Nuptse Jacket.

According to recent reports, it’s familiar, but it’s also practical—the kind of gift you feel good about because it’s going to get a ton of use. (And it can withstand the repeated wears.) The attached hood offers protection from biting winds, and the straightforward color options make it easy to pair with a variety of outfits, whether it’s something fun or part of a heavy bundling during the coldest days of winter. This is the perfect type of winter coat: warm but not too puffy.

In a recent development, the Zaneck Jacket is a great alternative to the Aconcagua, stepping away from the outdoorsy look the brand is best known for. It’s still waterproof and insulated, but it has a longer, more modern cut.

According to recent reports, the Zaneck comes with a removable faux fur lining for the hood, which, in addition to being warm, means there are a couple of different looks that can be teased out of it. The straight cuffs add to its stylish feel in a way that doesn’t scream “I’m dressed for warmth and not fashion,” even though it’s doing both.

The Lone Peak Triclimate 2 has a lot in common with the Zaneck. From a distance, they cut a similar silhouette. However, the Lone Peak adds a little versatility if you’re looking for a jacket that can handle a variety of climates.

A removable, insulated inner jacket is attached to a removable, insulated top layer, which is fit for rainy conditions or as a spring or fall jacket. The insulated layer converts the whole thing into a winter-ready jacket. It also sports underarm vents capable of releasing heat in the middle of a long hike, ideal for outdoorsy types. The hood is removable and it’s got adjustable cuffs and an adjustable hem, making this a do-it-all jacket.

It might be easy to ignore the Pertex Jacket. It’s a bit unassuming. It doesn’t cut as stylish of a figure as the Zaneck, but it’s endlessly useful. The lightweight Pertex fabric will keep you dry in a downpour, but it also offers warmth without marshmallow-like bulk.

Sources indicate that the lightweight aspect makes this the kind of coat you toss in the backseat on the way to a hike, just in case. It’s also great for layering, whether it’s tossed on over a sweater or layered under an overcoat to make a favorite jacket more winter-ready.

It has been revealed that this edition of the classic Base Camp Duffel echoes the design details we love in The North Face’s jackets. While it’s got enough style and a heap of color options for daily use, it’s built for adventure.

In a recent development, made with water- and tear-resistant fabric, it boasts 71 liters of storage space, a roomier option to the similar 31-liter version. Like all of the brand’s products, it’s built as if the designers have been through the rigors of outdoor adventures (and they probably have). It’s got a sweeping D-zip opening, backpack straps, mesh pockets, and compression straps in case you’re curious if you can pack 73 liters worth of gear into the 71-liter space. (You know you’ve tried.).

The North Face has a lot of hats, none more iconic than this. The Salty Lined Beanie has a classic feel, fitting snuggly over the head with rib-knit texture, a cuffed shape, soft fabric, and ample color options to ensure it will match any jacket or accessory. The Salty Lined Beanie encapsulates the entire The North Face vibe in a small way: It’s stylish enough for a subway ride to work and practical enough for an outdoor adventure. Best of all, it’ll keep your ears warm in either instance.

Industry observers note that often, the best glove is the one that disappears into the outfit. It looks seamless, keeping hands warm without drawing too much attention. The Etip Recycled Glove is about functionality first and foremost, but the simple design and understated colors makes it look good with a variety of winter outfits.

While we all like to pretend we aren’t attached to our phones, the Etip makes a great modern gift because its stretchy fleece delivers a snug fit and the palms have touchscreen compatibility. That means you won’t have to take off your gloves to respond to that key text while the snow is falling.

And this Black Friday, you can get the right tool for the job at the lowest prices of the year.

There’s a difference between owning an electric scooter you haul out the farmer’s market every few months and actually riding one every day. If you’re just covering the occasional trip around the neighborhood, almost anything with two wheels and a battery will probably do. But if you’re depending on your scooter to handle a hard commute climbing hills, navigating broken pavement, and covering serious distances ever day, the right equipment matters – and Ausom has the right equipment for just about any ride.

From November 16-December 1, Ausom’s has the right equipment making that decision a little easier this Black Friday, with its entire electric scooter lineup hitting its lowest prices of 2026 and additional savings available exclusively to Electrek readers when they use the code ElectrekFB at checkout.

Recent findings suggest that before diving into the individual e-scooter breakdowns, let’s first take a look at the flash sale deals available throughout the event. Industry observers note that with six different models on offer this shopping season, Ausom has the right ride for just about every kind of rider, from everyday campus commuters looking for dependable transportation between bells to high-strung adrenaline junkies ready to push the limits of tiny, two-wheeled performance. Industry observers note that built for real-world roads, the Gosoul 2 offers smooth, quiet, and confident travel across city streets, wet roads, and light gravel with puncture-resistant 10×2.5″ tubeless tires that reduce the risk of flats, enhance grip, and reduce maintenance needs for everyday dependability. E-ABS brakes cut motor power for faster responses and shorter stopping distances with superior control, while the powerful, 1100W motor, 70 km (~44 miles) of range, and ability to haul riders up 20% grade hills make the Gosoul 2 a great choice for any tech-savvy commuter.

Regularly priced at $729, the Gosoul 2 is on sale this month for just $569, and $549 for Electrek readers.

Sources indicate that for riders who want something more than basic transportation, the L2 Max Dual Motor brings serious performance to city streets, hills and gravel rides. A nearly 1 kWh battery provides up to 90 km (~56 miles) of range, making longer commutes and multiple stops around town easier to manage between charges. The 10×3″ puncture-resistant tubeless tires help maintain traction while reducing the risk of flats, and an adjustable dual swingarm suspension smooths out potholes, cracked pavement and rough gravel. With a top speed of 38 mph and the ability to tackle grades up to 34%, the L2 Max has plenty of performance in reserve for hard commutes and demanding rides, while its front and rear disc brakes with E-ABS help bring that power under control when traffic (or wildlife) demands a quick stop.

Regularly priced at $1,049, the L2 Max Dual Motor is on sale this month for $809, and $799 for Electrek readers.

Built for riders who refuse to choose between range and performance, the DT2 Pro packs dual 1,100W motors producing more than 2,900W of peak power. That’s enough muscle to tackle steep hills and grades of up to 36%, even when the route gets challenging, while its nearly 40 mph top speed gives riders plenty of acceleration for open stretches. The DT2’s 1.22 kWh battery delivers up to 115 km (~71 miles) of claimed range, making it a strong option for longer commutes or riders who want to cover several trips without stopping to recharge. Its 10×3″ puncture-resistant tires provide a wider contact patch for added traction, while an adjustable suspension front and rear helps absorb bumps, cracks, and rough patches to keep the rider stable and comfortable across changing terrain.

Regularly priced at $1,349, the DT2 Pro is on sale this month for $1,069, and $1,059 for Electrek readers.

Taking the Gosoul 2 to the next level, the Gosoul 2 Pro Dual Motor packs a pair of 1,400W motors for a 36 mph top speed and the ability to tackle grades of up to 33%. An 864 Wh battery provides up to 90 km (~56 miles) of range, while the Ausom ShocFree dual swingarm suspension and 10×2.75″ tubeless tires help keep things smooth and stable on all kinds of roads and paths.

Regularly priced at $999, the Gosoul 2 Pro Dual Motor is on sale for $829, and $799 for Electrek readers.

The K20 Pro Dual Motor packs plenty of performance into a more approachable package, with dual 1,400W motors delivering 2,800W of peak power – more than enough to give riders the go-power they need to carve up modern day traffic and tackle grades of up to 33%, while its 36 mph top speed leaves plenty of headroom for open stretches. Its 864 Wh battery provides up to 90 km (~56 miles) of claimed range, making it a practical option for hard commutes or a full day of riding around town. ShocFree suspension and 10×2.75″ tubeless tires help smooth out potholes, uneven pavement and light off-road sections, while front and rear disc brakes with E-ABS provide maximum control during emergency stops.

Regularly priced at $879, the K20 Pro Dual Motor is on sale for just $689, and Electrek readers can do even better at $679.

Just like it states on the tin, the F1 Max offers maximum performance inspired by the pinnacle of motorsport. Built for riders who want their electric scooter to be considerably more than a commuter, this one delivers up to 3,840W of peak power, pushing the F1 Max to speeds of up to 45 mph and allowing it to tackle grades as steep as 38%. A 1.25 kWh battery pack gives riders 100 km (~62 miles) of range, while an adjustable dual-swingarm suspension and 10×3″ tubeless tires give the scooter the hardware to handle everything from broken city pavement and gravel to light off-road trails. Hydraulic disc brakes with E-ABS help bring all that performance back under control, while a 330 lb. maximum load and wide deck make the F1 Max a substantial machine for bigger, bolder riders ready for longer trips into the wilderness and anyone looking for a little LOT more excitement from their electric scooter.

Regularly priced at $1,549, the Ausom F1 Max is available at the awesome price of just $1,429 for Electrek readers with code ElectrekFB.

Ausom isn’t done yet. They’re sweetening the deal for Electrek readers by throwing in a free gift with every scooter purchase. The Most Comfortable Sneakers for Women, Tested by a Style Writer

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Industry observers note that at this point, I’m pretty sure I qualify as the woman who lived in her shoes. Not in a glamorous Carrie Bradshaw kind of way, but in a professional-sneaker-tester kind of way. I probs have at least 30 pairs crowding my closet and entryways right now, and that’s not even counting the pairs I’ve run into the ground or given away to friends and family (you’re welcome). My top priority is always comfort, and while you might find that a given when it comes to sneakers, I’ve tested my fair share of options that make my feet feel stiff and achy.

Industry observers note that so, I present to you the pairs of comfortable shoes—think walking shoes and cross-training shoes—that actually keep me feeling comfortable and supported without slacking on cuteness. From memory foam insoles that mold to your foot's unique shape to running shoes with responsive soles that absorb your stride’s shock, these are the most comfortable sneakers for women, tested by myself and other sneaker enthusiasts at Women’s Health.

Recent findings suggest that the brand ethos of On is to make people feel like they're running on Clouds. It achieves this thanks to its signature Helion Superfoam midsole, which sets itself apart with a construction that blends rigid, stable sections with flexible foam. This combination of materials provides the perfect balance of cushioning and energy return, giving you a bouncy, lightweight feel when your foot hits the pavement. The result is a soft, natural ground feel, rather than an overly bouncy cushioning experience. Fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi says this tech alone is why this shoe is an absolute workhorse when it comes to running (and running fast!). It’s her all-time favorite race shoe—she even ran a half-marathon in it.

Sources indicate that according to Accardi, the shoe feels firm but still has enough flexibility that her running gait isn’t impacted. The toebox has a ton of room for movement, but still holds the foot in place so each step feels responsive and energetic. Even when her legs feel like they’re about to give out, these shoes pick her right back up. On’s innovative speedboard, a flexible plastic plate wedged between the footbed and midsole, snaps back into place for a bouncy effect after your feet hit the ground. This means the shoe requires less energy output with each stride, making running feel easier. Plus, the rebound that comes with the underfoot cushioning gives a spring in your step.

I might not run marathons like Accardi, but I love to wear this shoe for walking and casual jogs. The CloudTec system, which uses air pockets in the midsole (the layer between the insole and the outsole), to create the shoe’s cushiony feel, propels me forward with every step, kind of like walking on a trampoline. And while it’s great for getting your steps in, this shoe has that chunky look that’s super on trend right now. I love pairing it with tailored pants and a boxy T-shirt on top for that upgraded activewear vibe.

One thing to note, though, is the sole wears down fast, which we found to be disappointing, especially given that price tag. Accardi states the Clifton 10 has a better tread thanks to its thicker outsole designed for high-friction.

Read more: On Cloudmonster 3 Review.

Out of all the sneakers I’ve tried, I find myself wearing the Brooks Ghost Max 3—it’s the newest addition to the Ghost Max series—the most when I want to feel comfortable during walks or runs (yep, it can do both!). That’s because the rocker bottom sole, which has a slight curve to it like a rocking chair, helps propel my foot forward with less energy. Wearing it literally feels like walking on pillows.

In a recent development, with the most cushioning of any shoe on this list (and the most cushioning Brooks offers), it’s perfect for those who need extra support. Fitness contributor Talene Appleton claims it has extra plush, foamy cushioning, but even for a max cushioned shoe, it’s incredibly stable thanks to Brooks’ signature Guardrails technology, which is a broad base with two pieces of foam on either side of the heel. It reduces the rolling of the foot both inward and outward, so it cradles your foot in place without messing with your stride. According to Appleton, this combination is great for those with higher arches. After hours of walking, she doesn’t feel an ounce of pain or discomfort. And if you have wide feet or bunions, you’re in luck—this shoe comes in both wide and extra-wide options (huge win!).

According to recent reports, during testing, I did notice that there was some wear and tear on the shoe pretty early on (it had only been a few months of use). The material on the upper of the shoe wore out pretty quickly. While this knocked it down a few points in my book, its supreme comfort still kept this kick at the very top of my list. Plus, I love how many fun colors the shoe comes in—because running and walking should be fun, right?!

Read More: Brooks Ghost Max 3 Review.

According to recent reports, the Hoka Clifton 11 is a standout favorite among WH editors. After testing nearly every Hoka model, I can attest that the Clifton 11 reigns supreme for walking. I was also a fan of the previous Clifton 10, and the newest version feels very similar—just a smidge lighter and more springy. It is by far the most comfortable model in the series to date, and it’s earned a spot in my shoe rotation for its supportive yet flexible cushioning.

Sources indicate that the first major difference I noticed is how light the Clifton 11 feels. Even after wearing it for several hours at a time, it doesn’t feel bulky or clunky. Which makes sense: Hoka did shave nearly half an ounce off the weight compared to the 10. The toe box is slightly narrower, too, but it doesn’t feel tight or uncomfortable. I prefer the more secure fit because it kept my foot from sliding around without feeling cramped. If you like a little more wiggle room for your toes, I would suggest opting for the wide sizing, though.

Despite its lighter weight, it has a generous stack of foam padding throughout the midsole. That weightless yet cushiony feel makes it ideal for my longer walks throughout NYC. The shoe has a mild heel drop (the same as the previous model at 8 mm), which helps distribute pressure evenly across the foot.

Sources indicate that I also find that the foam absorbs impact well. My feet—unfortunately plagued by plantar fasciitis—never feel fatigued wearing this shoe. There's technically a rocker shape built into the sole, but it's subtle enough that I barely notice it—instead, my stride feels smooth and natural whether I’m walking or running. I’m also a fan of the durable rubber outsole that gives plenty of traction. I never feel like I’m going to slip while wearing these, even when walking down slippery subway stairs.

Recent findings suggest that so far, the Clifton 11—which was debuted alongside the fresh Clifton Pro— does a great job of keeping my feet comfy and supported. It’s a great shoe for anyone in need of a comfortable, everyday walking sneaker that can also handle the occasional jog (unlike the Clifton Pro, which is geared more toward high-speed running).

Read more: Hoka Clifton 11 and Clifton Pro Review.

There’s nothing worse than slipping into an uncomfortable shoe after a tough run—that’s where the Alo Recovery Sneaker comes in. Designed to support tired feet, it features a structured sole and high-rebound foam insole that offers arch support and bounces back into place with each step. It makes every step feel stable, cushioned, and balanced. The second I put this pair on after a long run, my feet are instantly relaxed. I can’t say that about most of my other sneakers.

One of the biggest perks of this shoe? The traction is next-level, which is key for a recovery sneaker that’s meant to keep you comfortable and steady all day. Inside, the sock-like lining prevents your foot from sliding around. The thick ankle collar also helps stabilize the foot and provides extra support up the leg, keeping everything locked in place.

It has been revealed that style-wise, this sneaker goes with everything—sweats, shorts, jeans, leggings, you name it. That’s why I crowned it the best overall platform sneaker. After giving it a spin for a few weeks running around Manhattan, walking my dog around Long Island, and wearing it to and from workout classes, it's done the best job at keeping my feet pain-free compared to many other platform sneakers I've worn. The 1.5-inch platform is subtle but adds just the right amount of height to elongate my legs without being so tall that I feel unstable. Oh, and it’s super cute to boot. I’m a substantial fan of the Natural White colorway, which looks clean and classic, and pairs effortlessly with everything from sweatpants to denim.

Even if you’re not fresh off a run, it works for the office, errands, or a casual lunch. It’s hands down one of the most versatile (and most worn) shoes in my closet. My one con is that it feels a bit heavy and bulky, especially after a long day of wear.

Read more: Alo Recovery Mode Sneaker Review.

Sources indicate that I hadn't tried Asics until this year, and now it's my go-to shoe brand. Not only does its shoe have a streetwear vibe (I'm loving the bright yellow color with sweats and jeans), but they’re also some of the most comfortable shoes I’ve ever worn. In the UB9-S Gel Kayano 20s, the brand uses its signature gel cushioning technology, which features gel units placed in both the heel and forefoot of the shoe to absorb shock and provide a soft landing. This cushioning adapts to your foot’s movement, offering flexibility while reducing impact on your joints. Plus, the form-fitting upper keeps your foot locked in place, making it perfect for long runs, but stylish enough for everyday wear.

I wear this shoe everywhere—on runs, in the gym, and even to the office—and I get compliments virtually every single time I step out in it. The support is unmatched, the traction is solid, and it’s lightweight enough that I never feel weighed down. Plus, it breaks in fast (I wore it right out of the box), so there’s no awkward adjustment period. If you’re looking for a sneaker that can do it all while still looking cool, this is the one for you.

In a recent development, one con to note: It comes in some funky colors, so if you’re not into something bright and fun, I’d recommend looking elsewhere. I also wish it came in a wider version for those with wider feet and bunions.

Read More: Asics Gel-Kayano 20 Review.

Sources indicate that we’ve been fans of the Chargefeel line for years, with the previous edition—the Chargefeel 2—winning the best cross-training shoe for our 2025 WH Sneaker Awards. Lululemon has since made a few tweaks that make it even better. “Everyone I know who has worked out in the Chargefeel—myself included—has loved its perfect balance of stability and flexibility,” indicates WH executive health and fitness director Jacqueline Andriakos, NASM-CPT.

In a recent development, now with a lighter weight and a lower heel-to-toe drop (6 mm compared to 9.5 mm), the shoe doesn’t weigh me down and puts less stress on the ankles and feet. I’m a significant fan of the wider base for lifting and squatting because it makes my feet feel locked. The forefoot-hugging band on the inside of the shoe and a tough plastic heel counter add extra security, while the springy EVA foam cushioning makes it a workhorse for walking and running.

According to recent reports, and post-workout, it’s a great leisure kick for traveling or running errands. I recently wore this sneaker while traveling, and it kept my feet happy power walking through the airport and standing in long security and customs lines. Andriakos agrees, stating, “The stylish silhouette looks good outside the gym.”.

The fit is true to size, and while wide-size options are not available, the toes still have adequate room to spread with each step or lift. However, the wide outsole may feel too bulky during stair climbing or quick, dynamic moves.

Read More: lululemon Chargefeel 3 Review.

Recent findings suggest that let me introduce you to my new favorite low-profile, fashion sneaker: the Puma Speedcat. It’s been making waves with style girls, and after testing it out for months, I can see why. This shoe pairs so well with any outfit, with a slim, almost ballet-flat silhouette that doesn’t clash with nicer pieces in my wardrobe. I even see celebs like Em Rata sport the Speedcat all the time, and they always make any streetwear ‘fit look so chic and cool.

It has been revealed that like the Samba, it has a pretty flat sole, but I actually find it more cushioned thanks to its EVA midsole, which has a lightweight, cushioned feel and shock-absorbing properties. This means I can walk around for longer without my feet aching. Plus, after wearing it on wet city streets, I’ve noticed it has better traction, which is a huge win.

In a recent development, the only downside? The fit is a little narrow, especially in the toe area. If you have wider feet, I’d definitely recommend sizing up.

Read More: Puma Speedcat OG Review.

Originally designed for indoor soccer, the Adidas Samba has become a cult-favorite sneaker that’s just as popular on the streets as it is on the field. At first glance, the Samba looks pretty flat, so I wasn’t expecting much in terms of comfort. But after logging hundreds of miles walking around the city, I was surprised by how well it supports my feet. The Samba uses a combination of synthetic leather for the upper and a rubber sole with a cushioned midsole for comfort. The cushioning is more subtle compared to high-performance running shoes, but it still provides a soft, supportive feel. Even without a ton of cushioning, I rarely experience discomfort, which is impressive for a sneaker this sleek. It runs narrow, especially for wide feet, and I recommend going a half size down, as it tends to run massive—many with wider feet or bunions agree it’s not the best fit.

It’s a go-to for effortlessly cool outfits—you can wear it with jeans, dresses, slacks, or shorts and always look stylish. I own this shoe in two different colorways (it comes in so many different shades), and after wearing it with practically everything in my closet, I can confidently say it adds a sporty, trendy touch to any outfit.

According to recent reports, one of Under Armour’s first-ever shoes, this kick is rooted in sport. But it’s gotten some essential upgrades since its launch, and it’s safe to say I’m hooked. Since 2009, it’s been updated with leather upper overlays to keep the foot supported and soft UA HOVR cushioning, made from soft EVA foam and rubber, which is engineered to store and release energy with each step, providing a bouncy, responsive feel that helps propel you forward. Out of all the shoes I’ve tried, this pair feels the most bouncy, which I know is an absolute essential for the runners and walkers out there that like that super thick underfoot feel. It also has a rocker shape to keep the foot in a forward motion for less energy exertion.

It has been revealed that the UA Apparition also has a mesh upper for supreme breathability—I’ve worn it during HIIT workouts, runs, and walks and never feel like my feet are constricted or sweaty, but I still feel supported and balanced. With a sleek, minimalistic look, the Apparition pairs well with anything from gym gear to casual streetwear. The rubber outsole provides traction and durability, allowing for smooth transitions during both dynamic workouts and everyday use.

My one con? There are some fun colors available, but I wish there were more options to choose from.

In a recent development, when it comes to comfortable sneakers, cushioning should be your top priority—whether you’re walking, running, hitting the gym, or just running errands. Here are the cushioning levels you can expect to see in the shoes below:.

As Women’s Health editors, we practically live in sneakers, so we know what it takes for a shoe to feel super comfortable. When I originally put together this list of the most comfortable sneakers in 2025, I spent over two years testing more than 50 pairs in every possible scenario—long and short walks, runs, HIIT workouts, full days out in NYC, travel days, and more. For this 2026 revision, myself and other WH editors re-tested newer iterations of our favorite pairs to make sure they still meet our standards. I also sought advice from fitness contributors Nicolette Accardi and Talene Appleton, as well as style contributor Lily Wohlner. We looked at everything from cushioning and stability to sizing, traction, and color options. And if a pair left our feet aching or uncomfortable, it didn’t make the cut. So you can trust that every sneaker on this list kept our feet happy all day long—even through our toughest workouts.

  • The slopject’s unsavory first cousin, the slopspace—a full-scale interior scheme, created through digital rendering, and now generative AI—is increasingly populating home-decor inspiration sites like this one, where a viewer can encounter improbable living scenarios like garage apartments with no ladders or stairs to reach the lofted bed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that can I interest you in an autonomous sauna rideshare? How about a conversation pit car? Or a Magic 8 Ball in the shape of Rick Rubin? How about a plate for a single almond or a toilet turntable?

Friends, do I even need to say it? These objects—or slopjects, as their creator calls them—are not real. Though they look convincing on the feed, they don’t exist in meatspace the way that you or I do. They are Dadaist fantasies, dreamed up and rendered digitally without the limitations of production budgets, market demand, or even those pesky things known as laws.

The slopject’s unsavory first cousin, the slopspace—a full-scale interior scheme, created through digital rendering, and now generative AI—is increasingly populating home-decor inspiration sites like this one, where a viewer can encounter improbable living scenarios like garage apartments with no ladders or stairs to reach the lofted bed.

With hyperrealistic renderings a mere prompt away (and disclosures of AI-generated content remaining spotty at best), it’s getting harder to tell what’s real. On platforms like Pinterest and Instagram, where homeowners often seek inspiration for their design projects, the speculative images that float through the digital ether can be particularly hard to detect. Entire subreddits are dedicated to sniffing them out.

And detection is just the beginning. Aside from struggling to detangle fact from fiction in stumbled-upon images, consumers are also using LLMs—or large language models, AI tools designed to work with human speech—to generate their own visions of their dream home, without always understanding what it takes to make those fantasies a reality. That dynamic is starting to have concrete consequences for the professionals charged with designing and building the rooms we live in, where dollars and cents, artisanal skill, and the laws of physics remain painfully real. (Just ask the guy who tried to exit the lofted bed without a ladder.).

“People are seeing or prompting more fantastical solutions that are not rooted in the reality of the built environment, and then they’re presenting those to us as something that can be executed,” indicates Kevin Greenberg, founder and principal of the AD PRO Directory–listed firm Space Exploration Design. “We do it diplomatically and we do it politely, but we will tell them, ‘Oh, you know, it’s really difficult to achieve a stone ceiling.’”.

Recent findings suggest that this change is happening fast. Stanford University’s 2026 AI Index Report notes that more than half of the population has started using generative AI in the past three years—a swiftness that outpaces both personal computers and the internet itself. When Midjourney and other AI imaging tools first hit the market, Greenberg indicates, clients used them to test the limits of what was aesthetically possible. “The prompt was like, ‘tropical Tudor fantasy,’ and then we were left to clean up the mess,” he recalls. “The images we were seeing were just tacky, and we all got a really big belly laugh out of it.” No one’s laughing now, he says.

In a recent development, these days, homeowners are feeding designer-created collages, mood boards, and sketches into Claude to see what spaces might look like once they’re built. The results tend to be uncanny: surfaces gleam like the Las Vegas strip, proportions are wonky, and there’s an unsettling feeling of dead air. Cy and Genevieve Carter, the principals of the Fresh York City–based interiors firm Carter Design, joke that the worst dig they can make on a space is to say it feels like standing inside of a rendering. In the world of AI images, “there’s not a simplicity of space,” notes Genevieve, which often means that more subtle textures like plaster don’t properly register.

Recent findings suggest that jake Shapiro, the owner of Hudson Valley–based millwork studio Slabrock, compares the images produced through AI software to the bloodless cuisine now rendered on deli signs. “It looks like scrambled eggs, but it also looks like H.P. Lovecraft, and that’s just horrific,” he states. “The same thing exists in design.”.

Sources indicate that there’s treachery in these images, designers agree, in that they portray a space nearly—but not quite—photorealistically. While that theoretically might help a homeowner understand how a designer’s vision for a space maps onto the real thing, it also bakes in a false sense of exactness that can leave room for misunderstanding or even disappointment. Organic materials like wood, for instance, can be difficult to predict with precision in AI. Every tree is different, Shapiro points out.

Catherine Campbell Pearson, a set designer and stylist based in Brooklyn, is seeing AI-fantasy expectations infiltrate the environments she designs for photoshoots too. In the past she and her clients would work from a “comp,” or a Photoshopped portrayal of the imagined end shoot. With those more lo-fi pictures, there was an understanding that the finished product would look slightly different. That’s disappearing in the age of GenAI: “It’s such a cohesive version of their idea that there’s much more attachment to the finished product looking exactly like this AI image.”.

This phenomenon has real consequences for designers, whose expertise is on the line when a rendering goes awry. When clients go off on their own and submit designers’ early proposals into AI platforms, “The rendering that it produces is really unsexy and clunky and ugly,” says Greenberg. “Then they’re looking at us like, ‘Well, you’re actually not that good at your job.’”.

Sources indicate that what these examples illustrate isn’t a new problem, exactly, but it is one that’s more apparent in the age of AI. Just as Pearson has relied on low-resolution comps to create environments in the past, designers often use tools like collage, drawings, and mood boards to gesture at vibe and design intent before progressing to a more dialed-in rendering. But most homeowners don’t have the language to communicate exactly what they want to a designer—and when they do, the language may not precisely match the listener’s interpretation. (One person’s “cozy” interior is another’s clutter-filled nightmare, just as one person’s “serene” oasis is another’s sterile dystopia.).

According to recent reports, LLMs offer clients a way to articulate their ideas in a way they may not have been able to otherwise—but in doing so, they create a highly specific rendering for a space that will require negotiation with real materials, labor, and budget—the latter being a serious constraint where AI can cause problems, says Tyler Polich, cofounder of the Los Angeles–based firm Years Studio. He shares an example of a client fiddling with an image and generating an element fully clad in copper—an option he and his partner would have never presented because of the cost. “Maybe it makes for a compelling image,” he concedes, “but we know that Gemini just blew their budget immediately.”.

In certain cases, these visualizations can simplify things for designers and clients. Lucca Zeray, the Berkshires-based maker of Lucca House modular shelving, has found the addition of an AI rendering tool—a “configurator” that can depict his brand’s color-edged units in the proportions they’re seeking and provide a cost estimate—to be a game changer in the ordering process. “It’s a way that we can be like, ‘Here, you draw it,’ and close the gap,” he says. Unlike the every-detail-on-the-table possibilities of a full interior design rendering, Zeray’s configurator is only manipulating a few straightforward options, which might be part of the reason for its success.

In a recent development, in the reality of a built design, image making is only a small piece of the puzzle. The real work is in executing—navigating the personal relationships, sourcing fabricators, and negotiating details with the give and take of material reality. “We don’t work just in ideas,” indicates Genevieve Carter. “We work in stuff and things, and people, and their expertise is still a dialogue.”.

It has been revealed that beyond the making itself, the design still needs to be good. Before AI was widely adopted, the algorithm-fueled flattening of taste was already in the cultural crosshairs. Social platforms reward likeable, heavily publicized images, like Athena Calderone’s marble-wrapped Brooklyn kitchen—photos that have been shared again and again. The problem then becomes that everyone is asking for an Athena Calederone–style kitchen. (It’s worth noting that even Calderone herself seems to have moved on from this look, by the way—her most recent home tour features a much moodier, Art Deco–inflected interior.) In today’s technological climate, this dilemma is taking a newly introduced form, as visuals take shape based on all of the environments that have been photographed and put online. But, says Polich, there’s an inherent flaw in this system: “The vast amount of visual information is relatively mediocre.” Real estate websites, DIY blogs, e-commerce images—most of the internet doesn’t look like, well, AD. It’s designed to be crowd-pleasing and just fine, not necessarily something extraordinary or innovative.

It has been revealed that years Studio similarly seeks to tease out its clients’ personalities—“something that is real and human and only exists in them,” as Polich puts it. That’s a vulnerable undertaking, but also one that AI cannot replicate when its foundation is built on remixing what’s already come before. Greenberg, the Carters, and Polich all recognize that there’s some element of a trust fall required on the client’s side. By the end of a project, a designer is often familiar with the most intimate details of their client’s life—even what they keep in their nightstand. (They see those specialty chargers, and they don’t judge.).

In a recent development, but in earning trust, ironically, AI is also occasionally lending designers an assist. For the Carters, an exacting client was reassured in the studio’s recommendation of a particular stone after she’d exhausted all of the other options herself in her AI engine of choice. Another time, they won over a prospect by tweaking his AI rendering, and suggesting color options the client hadn’t considered. Is it possible that Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini could remind homeowners why they hired a designer in the first place? Just ask the Rick Rubin Magic 8 ball: Signs point to yes.

#133130. Tesla Cybercab has crashed 8 times, and the data highlights a speed problem

Tesla Cybercab has crashed 8 times, and the data highlights a speed problem

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1189 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla’s Cybercab now has 8 crashes on file with NHTSA, barely two months after the purpose-built robotaxi started giving public rides in Austin.
  • In a recent development, four happened in driverless “Robotaxi” service, and none topped 5 mph.
  • The data points at what we think is the biggest limitation of Tesla’s self-driving program right now: speed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla’s Cybercab now has 8 crashes on file with NHTSA, barely two months after the purpose-built robotaxi started giving public rides in Austin.

In a recent development, four happened in driverless “Robotaxi” service, and none topped 5 mph. The other four happened with a test driver on board and Tesla’s driver-assist engaged, including one where a Cybercab hit a car at 53 mph on a highway in Philadelphia.

The data points at what we think is the biggest limitation of Tesla’s self-driving program right now: speed.

Tesla files Cybercab crashes under NHTSA’s Standing General Order in two separate datasets.

The first is the ADS (Automated Driving System) file, which covers Level 4 driverless operation. That’s the Robotaxi service, where nobody is in the driver’s seat. NHTSA’s latest ADS release, published this month, contains 43 unique Tesla reports, up from 22 in July. Four are Cybercabs:.

Industry observers note that those are minor. Two weren’t Tesla’s fault at all, and none involved an injury.

Recent findings suggest that the second bucket is the Level 2 ADAS file, which covers driver-assist systems like Autopilot and “Full Self-Driving” (Supervised). Tesla has been testing Cybercabs fitted with steering wheels and a human behind them, often in places where it has no Robotaxi permit. Those crashes land in the ADAS file, with the driver type coded “In-Vehicle (Commercial / Test)” and the system “Verified Engaged.”.

There are four of them, all in September 2026:.

In a recent development, tesla redacted the narrative of all four as confidential business information, so there’s no way to tell from the public data who was at fault or what the system was doing. Pennsylvania State Police, Austin Police, Lehi Police, and Florida Highway Patrol are listed as the investigating agencies.

The Philadelphia crash is not the Broad Street crash where a Cybercab lost its door panel that we reported in October. That one happened on a city street in October. This one happened on a highway in September, at around 10 p.m. local time.

According to recent reports, tesla has no permit to run automated vehicles in Pennsylvania, and it doesn’t run Robotaxi in Utah either. In Utah, a Cybercab was photographed in Park City in September with a driver visible behind the wheel.

It has been revealed that two of the eight Cybercab crashes involved injuries. Both are in the Level 2 file.

Industry observers note that across all 43 Tesla Robotaxi reports in the ADS file, the highest pre-crash speed is 29 mph. That was a driverless Model Y with two riders hitting a pothole in Dallas in September, after which one rider mentioned they sought medical care. The median speed across all 43 reports is 1 mph.

Industry observers note that not one of those 43 crashes happened on a highway. Tesla coded 21 on streets, 15 in parking lots, and 7 at intersections.

Industry observers note that those numbers say more about where Tesla lets the system drive than about the software itself. As we reported last month, Robotaxi sticks to low-speed routes inside small geofenced zones and largely stays off highways.

Recent findings suggest that the Robotaxi Safety Report Tesla published on October 21 claims zero people injured by Robotaxi over 3,112,541 driverless miles between January 22 and October 18. It doesn’t mention the Cybercab’s test fleet, and it excludes every mile driven with a safety monitor on board.

Take the speed cap off and the picture changes.

It has been revealed that in the Level 2 data, Teslas with Autopilot or FSD engaged regularly crash at highway speeds. Our master dataset of Tesla’s ADAS reports holds 69 fatal crashes. Among the 52 where Tesla recorded a speed, the median was 53 mph, the same speed the Cybercab was going in Philadelphia, and 29 happened at 50 mph or more.

Today alone, we matched three fatal crashes to Tesla’s latest filings:.

It has been revealed that engagement within 30 seconds of a crash, which is what triggers these reports, doesn’t prove the system caused it. But the pattern is consistent. At low speeds in a tight geofence, Tesla’s crashes are scrapes with chains, curbs, and potholes. At highway speeds, they can kill.

The Cybercab test fleet is where those two worlds overlap. It’s the same vehicle Tesla runs driverless in Austin, and the one Cybercab crash on record at real speed happened at 53 mph on a Philadelphia highway.

The Cybercab’s four driverless crashes are minor, and some weren’t Tesla’s fault. No one is denying that. But minor crashes still count, and so do the four Level 2 crashes that Tesla’s “zero injuries” framing leaves out. Both datasets describe the same vehicle running Tesla’s self-driving software.

It's looked to me for a while now that many of the improvements that people feel when they use FSD is not just the system getting better, but Elon pulling off the guardrails so the system attempts to do more stuff.

Industry observers note that what the data shows is that Tesla has a speed problem. Its Robotaxi service looks clean largely because Tesla keeps it slow, off highways, and inside small zones. That’s also what makes it far less useful than a real ride-hailing service. You can’t take a Cybercab to the airport if the airport is on the other side of a freeway.

To be clear, we think Tesla is right to do it this way. Given what the Level 2 data shows at 50+ mph, letting driverless Cybercabs onto highways today would be reckless.

In a recent development, but it means the hard part is still ahead. Highways, larger geofences, and higher speeds are where crashes become fatal, and that’s where Tesla needs its system to be nearly perfect before it can scale. The Cybercab’s test crashes suggest it isn’t there yet. The question is how long Tesla can keep growing a robotaxi network that can’t go fast.

Look for a light to medium level of compression for your yoga pants, Zoller says. Industry News: Adding wind cuts solar + battery storage power costs nearly 20%

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (781 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, solar and battery storage can do a lot of the heavy lifting in a renewable electricity system.
  • Wind fills gaps when solar output drops, so the system needs fewer batteries to keep electricity flowing.
  • Ember’s analysis, produced with the Global Wind Energy Council (GWEC), found that adding wind to solar and battery storage cuts the median cost of meeting 90% of electricity demand from $105 to $86 per megawatt-hour.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, solar and battery storage can do a lot of the heavy lifting in a renewable electricity system. Add wind, and supplying reliable power gets nearly 20% cheaper, according to latest analysis from energy think tank Ember.

Wind fills gaps when solar output drops, so the system needs fewer batteries to keep electricity flowing.

Ember’s analysis, produced with the Global Wind Energy Council (GWEC), found that adding wind to solar and battery storage cuts the median cost of meeting 90% of electricity demand from $105 to $86 per megawatt-hour.

The median cost of solar and wind power covering all demand is $89/MWh, with batteries and a little backup.

Solar and wind don’t follow the same schedule. Their output varies by time of day and across seasons, allowing one to offset the other’s shortfalls.

That matters because storing enough electricity to get through a long stretch of weak solar output gets expensive. Wind reduces the amount of energy the batteries need to store in the first place.

In the US, adding wind reduces the modeled battery requirement to meet 90% of demand from 20 hours of electricity use to 12 hours. Europe sees the same reduction, while China’s requirement falls from 18 hours to 12.

Sources indicate that the savings also put cheaper renewable power within reach of more regions. With wind included, regions that account for 75% of global electricity demand can meet 90% of their electricity demand at less than $100/MWh. With solar and batteries alone, that share is only 50%.

“We already know that solar and wind are cheap,” stated Daan Walter, principal at Ember.

By combining solar, wind, and batteries, we can deliver reliable power at remarkably low costs almost everywhere in the world. That’s a pretty fundamental shift in the economics of energy.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers also looked at prolonged periods of low output. Globally, weighted by electricity demand, a week of low solar output occurs roughly four times a year. A week in which both solar and wind output are low occurs only about once every four years.

In a recent development, that’s a global average, so individual locations will have different experiences. Ember defines a lull as seven consecutive days of output below half the source’s average.

Combining wind and solar reduces the gaps in low output.

The findings also raise questions for developers planning new fossil fuel plants.

Ember identifies 845 GW of coal and gas capacity in planning worldwide. Adding wind raises the share located in regions where solar, wind, and battery storage can meet 90% of demand for under $100/MWh from 71% to 90%.

In China alone, wind brings another 91 GW of planned coal and gas capacity into the range where renewables are cheaper.

Include backup to cover all demand, and 706 GW of the planned fossil fuel capacity sits in regions where the renewable-based alternative costs less than $100/MWh. Without wind, that figure falls to 520 GW.

For investors financing fossil fuel plants in the pipeline that are expected to run for decades, there is likely already a cheaper renewable alternative available to meet the same electricity demand, so it’s worth scrutinizing the project’s economics.

#133106. Latest Update: Tesla needs wireless charging fast, or its $30,000 Cybercab can’t charge at home

Latest Update: Tesla needs wireless charging fast, or its $30,000 Cybercab can’t charge at home

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1430 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla is now taking orders for the $29,990 Cybercab, with the first deliveries expected in Austin next month.
  • Sources indicate that the Cybercab has no onboard charger, so it only takes DC fast charging.
  • It has been revealed that when Tesla unveiled the Cybercab in 2024, Elon Musk said it wouldn’t even have a plug.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla is now taking orders for the $29,990 Cybercab, with the first deliveries expected in Austin next month. But there’s a problem buyers should know about: they won’t be able to charge it at home.

Sources indicate that the Cybercab has no onboard charger, so it only takes DC fast charging. And the wireless home charging pad Tesla has been teasing since 2023 still isn’t something you can buy.

It has been revealed that when Tesla unveiled the Cybercab in 2024, Elon Musk said it wouldn’t even have a plug. “It just goes over the inductive charger and charges,” he said on stage.

According to recent reports, that plan didn’t survive production, or at least the current version in production. Cybercabs have a NACS charge port behind a panel in the rear bumper, and Tesla has been plugging Cybercabs into regular Superchargers in Austin since they joined the fleet.

The bigger glitch is what sits behind that port. Tesla confirmed to attendees at Tesla’s Austin launch event in September that Cybercab has no onboard charger, the box that turns the AC power coming out of your wall into DC power the battery can store.

No onboard charger means no Wall Connector. No Mobile Connector on a 120V outlet, and no Level 2 station at the mall either. If it isn’t a DC fast charger, the Cybercab can’t use it.

For a robotaxi, deleting the onboard charger makes sense. It’s one less part to buy, cool, and carry around, and a fleet car spends its downtime at a depot, not in someone’s garage. Those little things help make the car more economical and efficient.

But Tesla is now selling the Cybercab to individuals.

Recent findings suggest that as we reported last week, Tesla’s Cybercab autonomy agreement requires a $299 monthly subscription for the car to move at all. The same document puts charging squarely on the buyer: “You are responsible for registration, insurance, parking, charging, general cleaning and all other costs.”.

It also tells owners to “keep the vehicle charged and connected so over-the-air updates can install.” Connected to what, it doesn’t say.

Recent findings suggest that the Cybercab Order Agreement limits the car to NACS DC fast charging, Superchargers included. It also says only the registered owner can use the Cybercab, and only while physically present in it for the entire trip.

The subscription agreement carves out one exception: when service is due, the Cybercab “will travel autonomously, unoccupied to a Tesla service center.” Nothing similar exists for charging.

So you can’t send your Cybercab to a Supercharger at 2 a.m. while you sleep, which is the one thing a self-driving car should be great at. You’d have to ride along, sit in a two-seater at a Supercharger while it charges, and ride back home.

The obvious answer is the wireless home charger Tesla keeps promising.

Tesla first showed what looked like a wireless home charging station during its Investor Day in March 2023. Later that year, chief designer Franz von Holzhausen confirmed the project on Jay Leno’s Garage, saying owners would “just drive over the pad in your garage” to start charging.

Tesla then filed patents for the charging pad and, after the Cybercab unveiling, released a video of it charging the robotaxi at 25 kW, claiming efficiency “well above 90%.” In February, the FCC granted Tesla a waiver to use ultra-wideband radios to guide the Cybercab onto the pad.

Sources indicate that and that’s where it stops. Tesla has never sold the pad, never priced it, and never given it a launch date. It even gave up on wireless charging for the Cybertruck last year, even though the truck shipped with the connectors for it.

With deliveries estimated for December, Tesla has about six weeks to launch a home pad if it wants the first owners to charge in their own garage.

Tesla’s own intends for Cybercab charging revolve around fleet depots. In Austin, it filed plans for a hub on St. Elmo Road with 48 V4 Supercharger stalls in a first phase and cabinets to support 80 wireless chargers in a second.

Tesla could, in theory, let private owners use it. But with the owner-presence rule, that means riding to a depot across town and waiting there. That’s a Supercharger visit with extra steps.

According to recent reports, the other route is a home DC charger, and those exist. We covered Sigenergy’s 25 kW bidirectional DC charging module last year, which bypasses a car’s onboard charger the same way a Supercharger does. Lunar Energy also confirmed a 25 kW home DC charger this year, but it’s not expected until mid-2027.

Recent findings suggest that neither is a plug-and-play answer. Sigenergy’s module is built to sit inside its SigenStor home battery system, which isn’t cheap, and Tesla would have to support third-party DC charging on a car it controls this tightly. Tesla could also build its own small DC wall unit. It hasn’t announced one, but CEO Elon Musk talked about integrating one into the Powerwall for years.

According to recent reports, this is what happens when you take a vehicle designed for a fleet and sell it to consumers to hit a deadline. And let’s be honest, charging is probably not even in the top 5 of problems with selling the Cybercab to personal owners in its current state.

Recent findings suggest that musk promised a Cybercab would be sold to a customer for under $30,000 before 2027. Technically, he’s going to make it. But on the Q3 earnings call, he also said “the vast majority” of Cybercabs will stay Tesla-owned and run as transport-as-a-service. The car was clearly engineered around that, and deleting the onboard charger is the best example.

Industry observers note that that saved Tesla money on every unit. The cost now lands on the few people buying one.

It has been revealed that I don't see any evidence that the production Cybercab has the onboard hardware to use such a pad. Besides the wireless receiver coil it would need some kind of charging hardware to convert the pulsed wireless charging into DC to charge the battery.

Industry observers note that if you live in Austin next to a Supercharger, you’ll manage. But think about what Tesla is actually selling here: a self-driving car that can’t drive itself to charge, can’t charge in your garage, and needs you sitting in it at a Supercharger. That’s worse than owning a Model 3 with a Wall Connector, and it costs $299 a month on top.

It has been revealed that the fix exists in Tesla’s labs. It has the pad, the patents, and the FCC approval. It needs to ship it as a product, ideally bundled with the car, or change the contract to let the Cybercab go charge on its own.

Will the first Cybercab owners get a wireless pad in December, or will they spend their evenings at Superchargers? And if it releases, how much will it cost? The rare few home wireless chargers that have been sold to date have been quite expensive, and the value proposition of the Cybercab, which is at the moment basically a $300 a month lease with a $30,000 down payment, is already pretty awful.

To Heal Your Heart, Purge Your Playlist

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1065 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in.
  • Recent findings suggest that since I was old enough to record playlists on cassette tapes, I’ve paired music with my intense crushes.
  • Recent findings suggest that I fell in love with my college boyfriend to the tune of Bruce Springsteen’s “Dancing in the Dark,” while Miles Davis’s Kind of Blue was the anthem that played throughout a 15-year situationship with an elusive artist.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Recent findings suggest that since I was old enough to record playlists on cassette tapes, I’ve paired music with my intense crushes. Each guy basically had his own song, sometimes an entire soundtrack.

Recent findings suggest that I fell in love with my college boyfriend to the tune of Bruce Springsteen’s “Dancing in the Dark,” while Miles Davis’s Kind of Blue was the anthem that played throughout a 15-year situationship with an elusive artist. Then, there was the whirlwind romance with a former smoke jumper turned ER doctor whose last concert was Emmylou Harris, which reminded me of the then-popular song “Emmylou” by First Aid Kit.

Each time, I became as obsessed with the song as the guy associated with it. My brain hyperfixated on the lyrics, first looking for hopeful clues, and then after the romance ended, sparking memories of sweet moments.

It has been revealed that music is often seen as a source of comfort for those dealing with heartbreak, but it can actually “arouse feelings of romantic longing, particularly searing melody,” says Walter Frisch, PhD, a professor of music at Columbia University. Some composers call such a haunting melody “l’idée fixe” or “fixed idea.”.

In a recent development, once that “fixed idea” gets stuck in your head—in the form of a song played on repeat—it can actually trigger the thoughts that land you in limerence, the involuntarily obsessive rumination on an idealized love interest. It’s fueled by both the hope that the person you like likes you back and the uncertainty of whether they do.

For a long time, I thought I was alone in my lyric-fueled limerence, but as I interviewed experts and other limerents as research for my memoir, When Longing Becomes Your Lover, I learned that it’s incredibly common—and normal—for our brains to connect music with unrequited lovers.

Sources indicate that neuroscience would call this melody intermittent reinforcement. When we are infatuated with someone, we are anticipating connection with that person, which results in our brain’s reward system releasing the “feel good” hormone dopamine. As a result, we are motivated to return to the behavior of deeply thinking, or ruminating, about them to get that reward.

In a recent development, in one famous MRI brain scan study, when heartbroken individuals were shown pictures of their heartbreakers, their dopamine pathways lit up just as they would from doing cocaine. Similarly, music can trigger someone to ruminate about what could be or what could have been with a romantic interest, says psychiatrist Jud Brewer, MD, PhD, the director of research and innovation at Brown University’s Mindfulness Center and author of The Craving Mind. The result, he says, is an itchy, contracted, restless feeling—quite the opposite of the expansive feeling associated with the mindfulness used to stop craving and anxiety.

Nostalgia also triggers the release of dopamine, and a song is like a time machine. Anytime I hear “Dancing in the Dark,” I’m instantly transported to kissing my college boyfriend in a dark, musty stairwell off campus. I can feel his hands resting on my hips and taste the Kentucky bourbon on his lips.

In a recent development, “There’s this certain charge you can get remembering somebody that you've been with before,” notes Geoff MacDonald, PhD, a social psychologist who studies singlehood and sexuality at the University of Toronto. “You can replay, sort of viscerally, what it felt like to have somebody who was into you [and] that has the potential to provide real validation.”.

Recent findings suggest that he points to one study on song lyrics and attachment styles that, he says, “provides some evidence that people are drawn to a self-reinforcing bubble when it comes to intimacy.” In other words, it’s a form of confirmation bias. You’re drawn to songs with lyrics that reinforce what you already think about relationships, and you’re more likely to read into those lyrics and apply them to your own life.

For example, if you have an anxious attachment style—which many limerents do—you typically feel insecure in relationships and fear abandonment. Consequently, you may need constant validation, which is exactly what a certain song can provide. When I heard “Emmylou” playing on the radio one morning after the sexy smoke jumper had grown more distant over text, I decided it was a sign from the universe that we were still meant to be together. (It wasn’t.).

So, what’s a forlorn lover to do? Purge your playlist. “When someone is addicted to a behavior, if they avoid the people, places, and things [associated with the behavior], they’re less likely to get triggered to do the behavior,” says Brewer. “It’s not a great long-term solution, but it's one step that they can take.”.

Think of songs that trigger you to ruminate, whether you’re obsessing over a crush or languishing over a lost love. Maybe it’s a song whose lyrics remind you of them, or a tune you danced to together. Whatever it is, consider removing that song from your playlist—at least until hearing the first few notes no longer rolls out you into a two-hour daydream about your love interest.

Now, if you've got a playlist that you play once every couple of weeks when you're feeling lonely, that can probably stay in your Spotify rotation. “It's good to remember that you can be loved,” MacDonald says. “But if you're leaning into that as a replacement for actually seeking real intimacy in your life, that's where you're going to run into problems.”.

Instead of relying on songs to dream about relationships that would never materialize, I deliberately poured that relentless energy into hobbies that gave my life purpose. That might look like spending quality time with a loved one, creating art, or planning a trip—anything that takes your mind off the individual and fills your self-worth bucket.

Now, I can listen to Kind of Blue and “Emmylou” without yearning for past lovers, but I prefer playing songs that reinforce the security I feel in my marriage, like “Ain’t No Mountain High Enough,” the song we walked down the aisle to.

Amanda McCracken is a journalist, writing professor at the University of Colorado, the author of When Longing Becomes Your Lover, and the host of The Longing Lab podcast.

When you're short on space (or even if you're not), having an extra set of drawers on hand is a huge boon for small bedrooms. That's where the best storage beds come in. I'm all about bedroom furniture that does more for your sleep setup, so I gathered up a few favorites from the AD staff. These storage bed picks include sleek, streamlined designs with completely concealed side storage, queen- and king-size beds with pullouts at the footboard, and more. Each one stows generously while you sleep.

In a recent development, A storage bed frame need not be ugly, even if function is the whole point of buying one. In fact, I tapped other editors and we found impressive wooden beds from Thuma and West Elm, the upholstered storage beds of our minimalist dreams from Saatva, Article, and Sundays, and a lilac velvet showpiece from CB2 for anyone who wants their storage bed to be the loudest thing in the room. The market has our back on this one, especially for those of us living in shoebox bedrooms where a queen bed barely fits, let alone a nightstand (the luxury). Below are the 10 storage beds I considered up to snuff, with editor commentary.

All prices in this article reflect queen-size beds unless otherwise noted.

All prices in this article reflect queen-size beds unless otherwise noted.

Bed frame reviewer: Kate McGregor, contributor.

Industry observers note that what attracted you to this bed frame? Like any girl living in Upcoming York in her mid-20s, I have a lot of stuff. And while I have ample closet space (a rarity), I like a certain level of type-A organization. Closed or hidden storage is key, and I didn’t want to fill my precious closet space with off-season sweaters and formalwear I reach for once a year. Enter: a platform storage bed. Not taking up any extra square footage was key, or else I would have bought a trunk or bookcase like my mother suggested. I had several coworkers who swore by Saatva’s mattresses for both quality and comfort, so investing in their furniture felt like a natural next step. The Halle bed frame is one of their more minimal silhouettes that I knew would suit my ever-evolving design style.

What was the delivery and assembly like? Delivery and assembly were a breeze. The team gave me an hour's notice before arriving, so I could prep my space (aka move my Amazon bed frame out of the way and vacuum). Assembly took about an hour, and the three-man team was incredibly efficient. They checked in with me multiple times throughout the process to ensure they got the placement exactly right. Afterward, they left with all the trash and packaging in tow, and they even helped me place my 150-pound mattress back onto the latest frame.

Are there any standout features? The lift mechanism is really much smoother than I'd expected. Durable linen handles ensure that I'm never fighting for grip on the base. If I'm really feeling it, I can lift the base with one hand to access the storage below.

What’s your bedroom design, and how does this storage bed align with your aesthetic? My bedroom is quite minimal—jute rug, dark wood dresser, cream linen curtains. I change my bedding at every whim, so I wanted a bed frame that wouldn't take up too much attention from my gingham sheets and block-printed quilt. The beige linen frame does just that, it serves as a neutral backdrop for whatever bedding layers I choose.

Did the bed frame live up to your expectations? Yes, and then some. Over the last eight months, this bed has remained sturdy, and without being too dramatic, it has revolutionized my apartment’s storage. Christmas garlands, high heels, and even craft supplies have all found a home in the spacious cavity. Plus, the raised base keeps all of my belongings off the ground. The linen fabric has softened a bit with age, especially on the headboard and handles that I’m touching more frequently than the frame. The lift mechanisms are easy to use and lock while lifted, allowing me to maneuver in the storage space without holding the bed up. The lift even handles my 150-pound mattress with ease, not even creasing a pillow.

Sources indicate that how would you rate the sturdiness of this bed frame on a scale of 1–10? The sturdiness is a 9/10—I dock it a point only because I pushed my bed frame and it shifted a bit away from the storage base. Otherwise, there's no movement, creaking, or stability concerns, even as I toss and turn.

Industry observers note that would you recommend this bed frame to a friend? Absolutely. This bed is a major investment, I won’t lie. But I don’t plan on needing a different bed frame anytime soon (maybe ever), so the longevity of this bed is well worth the price point.

Bed frame reviewer: Zoë Sessums, contributor.
